sens: The man who has begotten a child, his direct parent
The ancestor of a family or a people
One who founds, leads, or represents a group, a lineage, or a profession
One who protects, supports, and guides as a father would
A term of respect and honor towards an older man or a leader
God in His relationship of love and care towards His people
H0001G.detail: 1. The father is primarily the one who has begotten a child: "A man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife" (Genesis 2:24) signifies the natural bond and fundamental relationship between parent and child. 2. The word extends to more distant ancestors: "the God of your fathers," referring to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Exodus 3:16), reminding us of those from whom we descend and inherit. 3. A father can also be the founder or leader of a group: Jabal is "the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock" (Genesis 4:20), meaning he initiated this way of life. 4. The father represents protection and support: Job says he raised the widow "as a father" (Job 31:18), an image of one who nourishes and spares. 5. It is a title of respect given to an older or wise man — thus one greets a master or leader. 6. God Himself is called the father of His people (Exodus 3:16), evoking His constant love and vigilant care.
H0001G.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of producing, creating, giving life. In Hebrew, "father" is also the name of the first month of the calendar (later called Nisan), recalling the idea of beginning. The family of the word includes terms for "fatherhood" and "heritage." It is a very ancient word, present in Semitic languages in a nearly identical form, and it embodies a universal and primordial notion.
H0001G.emploi: This word appears more than 1,000 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis, which recounts the generations and God's promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It is concrete at first (the father of a child or a wife), then broadens: we speak of "fathers" to designate the founding ancestors of Israel (Exodus 3:16), of "paternal houses" for groups of families (1 Chronicles 23:24), and even of a "father" of a trade or class (Genesis 4:20-21, where Jabal and Jubal invent arts). In the prophets and psalms, the term also becomes spiritual: God is the father who protects and forgives. This progression of meaning — from genealogical link to relationship of trust and dependence — runs throughout Scripture.
H0001G.portee: Understanding "father" in the Bible invites the Christian to honor authority and transmission ("Honor your father and your mother"), but also to grasp God's love as a complete fatherhood: creator, protector, guide towards maturity. It is a key word for accessing the biblical image of God — not distant and frightening, but close, benevolent, and responsible for the destiny of His children. It also reveals the importance of generations and the link between past, present, and future in God's plan.

sens: who has competence and know-how in a field
H0001H.detail: 1. The word describes a person endowed with practical competence and know-how. In 2 Chronicles 2:13, King Hiram sends to Solomon a worker "skilled and intelligent" for the work of the Temple: this is someone who knows his trade, understands the techniques, and can execute complex tasks with mastery.
H0001H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to understand" or "to have intelligence." It expresses less scholarship than practical ability to grasp how to do something and to accomplish it. It is an intelligence of action rather than theory.
H0001H.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the context of the construction of the Temple. In 2 Chronicles 2:13, King Hiram the Phoenician uses it to describe a craftsman sent to Solomon. In 2 Chronicles 4:16, this same craftsman (also called Huram-abi) is designated by the same term. He is a highly talented worker, a specialist in bronze and metal work for the sanctuary.
H0001H.portee: This word reminds us that God honors skill and competence in the service of His Temple. Practical intelligence — knowing how to do things well — is a form of wisdom that God values. For the believer, this shows the importance of cultivating excellence in our labors.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the united monarchy
Father of Kish and several other children
H0001I.detail: 1. Abiel is a man of the tribe of Benjamin who lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He is first mentioned in 1 Samuel 9:1, where he is introduced as the father of Kish, the man from whom King Saul was born. 2. He was married to Maacah and had many children: Kish, Ner, Abdon, Zur, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zecher, and Mikloth. His name means "my father is God" in Hebrew, which shows the importance of faith in the families of Israel at that time. 3. Abiel is also called Jeiel in the text of 1 Chronicles 9:35, and sometimes Ner according to other biblical genealogies (1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:39), reflecting the variations of proper names in ancient genealogies.
H0001I.origine: The name Abiel comes from Hebrew and literally means "my father is God" (composed of av, "father," and el, "God"). This theophoric name, which contains the name of God, was common in Israel and expressed the family father's trust in divine protection. Biblical genealogies mention him in different forms, showing how names could vary slightly in the transmission of texts.
H0001I.emploi: Abiel is primarily mentioned in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8:29 and 9:35, where his descendants are listed in detail. He is the father of Kish, who became the father of King Saul, making Abiel an ancestor of the first royal dynasty of Israel. His importance lies mainly in his place in the royal genealogy rather than in specific accounts of his actions. The parallel texts of 1 Chronicles show that priestly genealogies were carefully preserved and transmitted to establish the lineages of important families in Israel.
H0001I.portee: Abiel reminds us that obscure and little-known ancestors of the believer may have had crucial importance in God's plan. Although he does not have a grand role recounted in Scripture, it is through his descendants that a king of Israel was born. This invites the reader to consider that God often works through generations without noise or visible human glory.

sens: direct male parent, one who has begotten
ancestor, man of the previous generation
author or founder of a dynasty or institution
one who exercises authority and protection like a father
God himself, as a spiritual father
H0002.detail:
1. The father is primarily the parent who has begotten a child: this is the simplest meaning, as when Belshazzar speaks of Nebuchadnezzar, his father in the strict sense (Daniel 5:2).
2. The word extends to more distant ancestors, to all those who have preceded us: the Hebrews speak of "their fathers" to refer to their ancestors who revolted long ago (Ezra 5:12).
3. The father can also be the founder or initiator of a lineage: Nebuchadnezzar is called "father" by his royal successors, thus showing that he is the origin of their power.
4. The father represents benevolent authority and protection: a father provides, guides, corrects. This is why one can say of a leader that he acts as a father towards those he governs.
5. The term also applies to God in a spiritual relationship: Daniel invokes him as "God of my fathers" (Daniel 2:23), recognizing that God is the supreme protector and guide, just as a father is for his child.
H0002.origine: This Aramaic word is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word אָב (av, "father", H0001), which shares the same root. Aramaic and Hebrew are two very closely related languages, and this word belongs to the fundamental vocabulary of both. The root evokes the idea of one who begets and ensures the continuity of life and protection. Throughout the Bible, the father is the symbol of creative power and benevolent governance.
H0002.emploi: This Aramaic word appears mainly in the Aramaic passages of Daniel and Ezra, which date from the late period of the Persian kingdoms. It first designates the biological father (Nebuchadnezzar father of Belshazzar in Daniel 5:2), then ancestors more generally ("your fathers" in Ezra 5:12, referring to past generations). It also applies to kings who founded a dynasty or established a political order: thus Nebuchadnezzar is "father" to his royal successors, meaning the one from whom authority emanates (Daniel 5:11, 5:13). Finally, it takes on a religious dimension when God is called "God of our fathers" (Daniel 2:23), which means that God has shown himself faithful to the lineage of believers since the beginning.
H0002.portee: The word "father" reminds us that every man depends on a chain of generations: we are indebted to those who have preceded us, and especially to God who is the father of all. By calling God "God of our fathers", the believer acknowledges that God is faithful through the ages and that he guides his people from the beginning. This invites everyone to respect the heritage of faith received and to see in God not a distant master, but a benevolent father who cares about the lives of his children.

sens: The freshness and green color of vegetation
The young shoots or tender leaves of plants
The lush appearance of a valley or a fertile garden
H0003.detail: 1. The word designates the green color and fresh appearance of living vegetation. In Job 8:12, the water grass is described as "green" (green in French), at the moment it grows: it is the image of youth and life. 2. It also evokes young leaves or tender shoots, those that are still full of sap and not dried out. It is this quality of freshness that constitutes greenery. 3. In a figurative or poetic sense, the word describes the beauty of a fertile and vibrant landscape: in Song of Solomon 6:11, the "greenery of the valley" is what makes the garden and the vines beautiful to behold, a sign of abundance and prosperity.
H0003.origine: The Hebrew word אֵב comes from a root that expresses the idea of greenness and freshness. Its Aramaic equivalent (אֵב, ev) means "fruit", showing the connection with the idea of growth and plant fertility. The root refers to everything that is tender, alive, and in full growth in nature.
H0003.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 8:12, Bildad uses it to describe the water grass at the moment it is still green and full of life, before it quickly dries up: it is an image of the vanity of what seems prosperous but disappears quickly. In Song of Solomon 6:11, the greenery of the valley evokes the beauty of a fertile and flourishing landscape, in contrast to the desire to check that the vines and pomegranates are developing. In both cases, the word paints the image of vibrant and lush vegetation.
H0003.portee: This word reminds us of the beauty of creation and the image of life in full growth that God intended. It invites us to contemplate nature as a sign of freshness and renewal. But it also warns us, through Job, that this greenery can disappear quickly: it is beautiful, but fragile and fleeting.

sens: Edible production of a tree, what it bears and provides for food
What nourishes, what sustains living beings
H0004.detail:
1. The fruit is what a tree produces, what can be seen and picked from its branches: the food it offers. In Nebuchadnezzar's vision in Daniel 4, the giant tree has "abundant fruits" (Daniel 4:12): this is concretely what it bears, what makes it useful and nourishes all living beings that approach it.
2. By extension, the fruit is also what sustains life: what allows each creature to subsist. The tree from which one must "scatter the fruits" (Daniel 4:14) is not only beautiful for its foliage, it is vital because it nourishes. This is why "every living being" draws its food from it (Daniel 4:21): the fruit is a source of life.
H0004.origine: The Aramaic word אֵב comes from the same root as the Hebrew אֵב ("greenery, youth of plants"). It primarily designates the vitality and youth of vegetation, that moment when the plant greens and becomes fruitful. The fruit is its culmination: the life of the tree that gives itself as food.
H0004.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Bible, all in the account of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4. The king sees in a dream an extraordinary tree with abundant fruits that nourishes all the animals. The word designates each time what this tree produces and offers: first its beauty and abundance (4:12), then what must be scattered when it is cut down (4:14), finally what characterizes its lost splendor (4:21). The fruit is always linked to the idea of fertility, utility, and life given.
H0004.portee: This word reminds us that divine creation is not barren: it produces and nourishes. The fruit symbolizes God's generosity, his will to provide for the needs of his creatures. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize in the gifts received the benevolent hand of the Creator who provides for all.

sens: Eunuch in the service of King Ahasuerus in Persia
H0005.detail: Abagtha was one of the seven eunuchs who served directly under King Ahasuerus, the Persian sovereign during the exile. These eunuchs held positions of trust at the royal court and executed the king's orders, especially during grand royal banquets (Esther 1:10).
H0005.origine: The name Abagtha means "given by God" or "gift of God" in Hebrew. It is a Persian or Middle Eastern name borne by an officer of the Persian court, attested only in the book of Esther which recounts the story of the Jews under the reign of Ahasuerus.
H0005.emploi: Abagtha is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Esther 1:10, where he is cited as one of the seven eunuchs of King Ahasuerus. His name appears in the list of royal officers whom the king ordered to bring Vashti before him during a feast. He represents the important servants of the Persian court, although the text provides no details about his actions or role beyond this mention.

sens: Cease to live, die
Be destroyed, annihilated, completely disappear
Be lost, misplaced, out of reach
Cause someone's death, destroy
Lose all value, become vain or useless
H0006.detail:
1. **Cease to live, die**: the word describes physical death or extermination of a person or group. In Esther 3:9, it refers to the destruction of an entire people; in Job 4:9, it is death caused by God's anger.
2. **Be destroyed, annihilated, completely disappear**: this is the total ruin of something: a city, an empire, a power. Exodus 10:7 describes Egypt perishing under the plagues; Isaiah 29:14 speaks of wisdom perishing, meaning it fades away.
3. **Be lost, misplaced, out of reach**: something precious that cannot be found. In Deuteronomy 22:3, it is a possession that has been lost; in 1 Samuel 9:3, it refers to the donkeys of King Saul that have disappeared.
4. **Cause someone's death, destroy**: a voluntary or divine action to annihilate an enemy or punish. Deuteronomy 7:24 speaks of the destruction of enemy kings by the Lord.
5. **Lose all value, become vain or useless**: in a figurative sense, wisdom or intelligence that collapses and serves no purpose. Deuteronomy 32:28 describes a nation that has lost common sense, which can no longer understand or act wisely.
H0006.origine: The verb אָבַד (avad) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to disappear" or "to go away." In Hebrew, the word can take three forms: the simple form (Qal) describes the action suffered (perish, be destroyed), the intensive form (Piel) makes it a voluntary action (destroy, cause to perish), and the causative form (Hiphil) emphasizes the devastating effect (cause destruction). It is one of the key words to express divine judgment or complete ruin in the Old Testament.
H0006.emploi: The verb אָבַד appears 174 times in biblical Hebrew, very frequently in Deuteronomy (which speaks of threats against Israel), in the Psalms (prayers for the destruction of enemies), and in historical books. Its meaning varies according to context: it can describe natural death or divine ruin, the annihilation of an enemy or the loss of a possession. In the threats of Deuteronomy (7:24, 28:63, 30:18), it carries a formidable gravity: it is the fate awaiting Israel if it abandons its God. In the Psalms, it expresses the hope that God will destroy the wicked (37:20, 83:18). In the account of Esther, this verb structures all the suspense: the plot aims at the destruction of the Jews, but it is ultimately Haman who perishes. It is a word of ultimate stakes: life or death, survival or annihilation.
H0006.portee: This word reminds the believer that in the Bible, the stakes are absolute: there is a radical difference between life that is built and destruction that is completed. It calls to take seriously God's promises and warnings. For the people of the Old Covenant, to perish meant exile and the end of worship; for the believer today, it invites reflection on what truly loses its meaning without God, and on the security that obedience to His word provides.

sens: Cease to exist, be destroyed definitively
Disappear, vanish without a trace
Be put to death, executed
Be reduced to nothing, completely annihilated
H0007.detail:
1. The primary meaning is complete annihilation: something ceases to exist. The false gods of the nations "will disappear from the earth" (Jeremiah 10:11), meaning they will leave no trace, they will be forgotten. It is the image of something that fades away, that is no longer anything.
2. In the context of people, the word means to be put to death: the king orders that "the wise men of Babylon perish" (Daniel 2:12), meaning they be executed. Daniel pleads: "Do not let the wise perish" (Daniel 2:24), so that this death sentence may be revoked.
3. The word can also express the destruction of a power or reign: the beast (the political beast of the vision) "was annihilated" (Daniel 7:11), its dominion "will be destroyed and annihilated forever" (Daniel 7:26). It is the total overthrow of a force that seemed powerful.
H0007.origine: The Hebrew word אֲבַד (avad) comes from a root expressing disappearance, annihilation. It describes the state of that which ceases to be, to exist, or to function. The word belongs to the vocabulary of judgment and ruin: it is often associated with prophetic threats and the end of God's enemy powers. In the Aramaic text of Daniel (Eastern Mediterranean dialect), it carries the same meaning as in classical Hebrew.
H0007.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the provided Bible, only in the later prophetic books (Jeremiah and Daniel). It is used mainly for death threats (disappearance of idols, execution of the wise) or definitive destruction (annihilation of the beasts of judgment). The context is always one of irrevocable end: no recovery, no return. In Daniel 2:12-24, the word appears three times to emphasize the gravity of the royal sentence and the urgency of the plea for mercy. In Daniel 7:11-26, it underscores that God's judgment against opposing powers is final.
H0007.portee: This word reminds us that the forces opposing God — false gods, wicked kingdoms, any power that rebels — cannot endure. They will be annihilated. It is both a threat to those who reject God and a comfort for the believer: God has the final word, and what seems invincible will be reduced to nothing. That is why faith invites us not to fear those who threaten the body, but to rely on God's eternal justice.

sens: Ruin, disappearance, annihilation of a person or a nation
State of one who is lost, condemned to disappear
Inevitable end, fatal destiny
H0008.detail:
1. The word describes the total ruin of a person or people: the nation of Amalek, in Numbers 24:20, is described as destined for destruction, meaning its complete annihilation. It is a state of irreversible disappearance.
2. It evokes the idea of being lost, falling under the weight of an inevitable fate. When the Bible says that someone will be "destroyed," it means they are condemned, that they cannot escape their end.
3. The word also carries a nuance of fatality: it is a destiny that is fulfilled, often announced in advance, like the Assyrian in Numbers 24:24, whose humiliation and destruction are events that will occur.
H0008.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to lose" or "to be lost." It is related to verbs that express loss, misplacement, or annihilation. The central idea is that of something or someone that disappears, that no longer exists — first in the sense of physical disappearance, then in the sense of end, annihilation.
H0008.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, both times in the prophetic words of Balaam in Numbers 24. It is used to announce the impending destruction of peoples: first Amalek (Numbers 24:20), designated as one who will be destroyed despite its status as the first nation, then the Assyrian and the Hebrew (Numbers 24:24). In both cases, the word expresses a divine judgment announced in advance, a sentence of disappearance that will be fulfilled. It is a term of prophecy that reveals the final fate of those who oppose God's people.
H0008.portee: This word reminds us that God controls history and the destiny of nations. It invites the believer to see that human powers, even the most imposing, are never safe from divine judgment. It also encourages placing trust not in the strength of enemies, but in the word of God that determines events with certainty.

sens: Something that can no longer be found, that has been misplaced
A possession entrusted to someone who loses or damages it
An object found whose owner is unknown
H0009.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a concrete, material thing that has been lost sight of: a misplaced garment, an animal that has escaped. In Exodus 22:9, it concerns judging between two people disputing the possession of a lost object, just like with an ox or a lamb.
2. It can also refer to a possession that someone has received in deposit or trust and that has disappeared or been damaged through their fault. Leviticus 5:23 lists: what he has stolen, what he has taken by fraud, what has been entrusted to him in deposit, and what was lost and he has found — all ways of not returning what does not belong to him.
3. Finally, it is any object found on the ground whose owner is unknown. Deuteronomy 22:3 commands to return to your neighbor any object that he has lost and that you find, such as a donkey or a garment.
H0009.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root אבד (avad), which means "to perish, to be lost, to disappear." Avadah is its verbal noun: literally, "the action of being lost" or "that which has been lost." It is a neutral form, describing the state of a lost thing without moral judgment on who is responsible.
H0009.emploi: This term appears four times in the Torah, always in legal contexts concerning restitution and honesty. In Exodus 22:9, the text settles the dispute between two people claiming the same lost object. In Leviticus 5:22-23, it appears in a list of violations of another's rights: denying having found a lost object is a sin that requires restitution with interest. In Deuteronomy 22:3, the law commands to actively seek to return anything lost to its owner. The word is always used in a context of integrity and civil justice.
H0009.portee: This vocabulary reminds the Christian reader that God cares about righteousness in small matters: a lost object is not a negligible detail. The intention to return what has been lost, even at the cost of difficulties, shows how Scripture elevates everyday honesty to the level of serving one's neighbor and faithfulness to the Law. It is a practical lesson on conscience and integrity.

sens: Place of destruction and death
Unfathomable depth where beings sink
Chasm of perdition
Insatiability and endless engulfment
H0010.detail: 1. The word designates a place of destruction and death, the abode of the dead in biblical thought. In Proverbs 27:20, the abyss is mentioned alongside the abode of the dead as a place that can never be satisfied: it continually engulfs and gives nothing back. 2. It is an unfathomable depth, a bottomless chasm from which no one returns. The image evokes a gaping mouth that devours everything thrown into it, never being filled. 3. The word can also refer to perdition, the state of those doomed to destruction, separated from God. 4. By extension, it represents insatiability itself: a need or desire that devours endlessly, always engulfing more without bringing satisfaction, as shown by the eyes of man eager for new riches.
H0010.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to perish" or "to be destroyed." It is formed to designate the place or state of destruction, the destination of those who perish. The term belongs to the vocabulary of death and divine judgment in the Old Testament.
H0010.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 27:20, in a context of wisdom that compares human insatiability to that of the abyss and the abode of the dead. The meaning remains constant: a chasm of engulfment that can never be filled. This powerful image illustrates the vanity of limitless human desires.
H0010.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the nothingness that a life without God can become, on the insatiability of carnal desires that devour us from within. It reminds us that only the Creator can truly satisfy our thirst, and that seeking satisfaction in the things of the world amounts to throwing oneself into a bottomless chasm.

sens: the underworld, the abode of the dead
destruction, annihilation
H0011.detail: 1. Abaddon is a Hebrew name that designates the underworld, the abode of the dead, often presented as a place of ruin and forgetfulness. In Job 26:6, the text states that "Abaddon is naked before God," showing that this hidden place does not escape divine scrutiny. It is a place where silence reigns and where the living can do nothing. 2. The word also evokes the idea of destruction and total annihilation. In Job 31:12, it speaks of a fire that "devours even to Abaddon," meaning that it completely ruins. In Proverbs 15:11, "Abaddon and the abode of the dead are before the Lord," associating this term with death itself and what it destroys in man.
H0011.origine: Abaddon comes from the Hebrew root אָבַד (abad), which means "to perish, to be destroyed." The name thus carries the idea of destruction and end. It is a specifically Hebrew word, without a simple equivalent in Greek, although the New Testament directly borrows it to designate a destructive angel in Revelation.
H0011.emploi: This word appears five times in the Old Testament, only in the wisdom books: Job (three times) and Psalms and Proverbs (once each). In these texts, Abaddon is not a character or a god, but a concept: the underworld where the dead lie forgotten, or the total destruction that threatens one who turns away from God. The biblical authors mention it to remind us that even the most hidden places, even death itself, remain under God's gaze and subject to His justice.
H0011.portee: Abaddon reminds believers of a humbling and liberating truth: no place escapes God, not even the grave or destruction. For the Old Testament, it is a call not to fear invisible powers, for God sees and controls them. This conviction sheds new light on death and the afterlife: they are not independent realms but remain under the Creator's control.

sens: The violent and complete end of a person or thing
The death or annihilation of an enemy
Irreversible ruin
H0012.detail: 1. The word designates complete and violent destruction: it is the total end, the definitive disappearance of a person or group. In Esther 9:5, when the Jews "destroy" their enemies, it is by the sword — a radical destruction, with no escape. 2. In a conflict context, the term specifically evokes the death of adversaries: it is not just falling ill or aging, but being struck down, annihilated by violence. This is why the same verse speaks of "striking" and "destroying" together: it is the definitive elimination of a threat. 3. The word carries a shade of irreversibility and fullness: one who "perishes" in this way has no hope of return. It is the fate of mercilessly defeated enemies.
H0012.origine: The Hebrew word אַבְדָן (av.dan) comes from the root אָבַד (ava.d), which means "to be lost, to disappear, to perish." It is a nominal form expressing the state or action of destruction. The same root appears in Hebrew verbs and adjectives describing ruin or loss. The concept evokes the idea of something that goes away, that does not return — a total loss.
H0012.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Esther 9:5. It precisely describes the moment when the Jews defend themselves against those who persecuted them during the days of Purim: they do not merely fight, but inflict complete destruction on their enemies. This historical and dramatic context shows that the term applies to the radical elimination of an existential threat, in the context of legitimate defense.
H0012.portee: This word reminds readers that the Bible does not hide the reality of conflict and violence: sometimes, the destruction of God's enemies and His people is presented as just and necessary. For a believer, this invites reflection on divine justice, legitimate defense, and the limits of mercy in this world — serious questions that require careful reading of the context.

sens: total annihilation, complete loss
ruin of a people, a nation
irreversible disappearance
H0013.detail:
1. The word denotes complete annihilation, the total loss of something — here, the definitive disappearance of a people. It is a strong word that evokes not just simple damage, but total erasure.
2. In the context of Esther, it refers to the ruin of an entire people: in Esther 8:6, the queen speaks of the "destruction" that would threaten the Jews under Haman's death decree. It is the annihilation of her entire nation that horrifies her.
3. This word carries the idea of an irreversible and total loss, more serious than a simple defeat or setback — it is the definitive end.
H0013.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root אבד (avad), which means "to perish, to be lost, to be destroyed." This root evokes the idea of disappearing, of vanishing. The suffix -ān (-ان) forms an abstract noun expressing the action or state of destruction. The same root can be found in other Hebrew words denoting loss or ruin.
H0013.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Esther 8:6. It designates the terrible fate that Queen Esther fears for her people: the total extermination ordered by Haman's decree. The uniqueness of this usage makes it a particularly solemn and dramatic term, reserved for this extreme situation where an entire people is at risk of disappearing.
H0013.portee: This word reminds us that the total destruction of a people is a feared reality that God's Providence can prevent. For the believer, it illustrates how human plans of evil can be thwarted by God's intervention — as shown in the continuation of the book of Esther, where the Jewish people are saved. It is also an invitation to take spiritual threats seriously and to rely on divine protection.

sens: To be willing to do something, to accept to do it
To consent to a request, to comply
To desire, to want something
To obey, to submit to a will
H0014.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses the inner disposition to carry out an action: to be ready, to accept. This is seen when Abraham's servant asks if the woman "will" follow him (Genesis 24:5), meaning if she will consent to this condition of the journey.
2. It can also indicate refusal, the absence of will: Pharaoh "would not" let the Israelites go (Exodus 10:27), and Saul refused to obey God's command regarding Agag (1 Samuel 15:9).
3. In a context of relationship with God, the word takes on a shade of obedience or disobedience: Israel "did not obey" the voice of the Lord (Psalms 81:12), which means that it refuses to submit to divine will.
4. God himself "wants" or "does not want": the Lord "did not want" to destroy Israel despite its unfaithfulness (2 Kings 13:23), showing his grace and faithfulness to his covenant.
H0014.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of consent and disposition of the heart. The family of the word includes other terms related to will and desire. The basic image is that of someone who accepts or refuses a request: it is an inner movement that manifests itself in word or action.
H0014.emploi: This verb appears 52 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives and the teachings of the prophets. It is used for characters refusing to obey God (Israel in Ezekiel 3:7, Pharaoh in Exodus 10:27), for human beings refusing one another (Saul refusing to spare Agag), and for God himself showing his patience or mercy (2 Kings 13:23). The word can also translate a positive acceptance: consenting to a covenant, accepting a proposal. Its meaning slightly changes depending on the context, oscillating between simple disposition of mind and moral obedience to authority.
H0014.portee: This word highlights the reality of free will — ours and God's. For the believer, it shows that obedience to God is not a fatality, but a choice of the heart. At the same time, it reveals that God does not force his will: he asks for our consent. Recognizing that we have the power to say "no" to God, but that his grace invites us to say "yes," transforms our understanding of the relationship with him.

sens: to express an intense desire, a passionate wish
to implore someone insistently to do something
H0015.detail:
1. The word evokes the expression of a deep and pressing desire, an inner longing that seeks to manifest itself. In Job 34:36, Eliphaz ardently wishes that Job be tested to the end, which shows the strength of this feeling: it is an intense wish, not a mere preference.
2. It can also mean to implore or beg someone to do something, with the idea of an insistent request that expresses this ardent desire. The phrasing "Let him continue then" in Job reflects this supplication mixed with wish.
H0015.origine: The Hebrew word אָבִי comes from a root expressing desire and longing — the aspiration of the heart that finds no rest. This root belongs to the family of words describing the intimate movements of the soul: desire, respectful fear, deep feelings that move a person.
H0015.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 34:36. In this passage, Eliphaz uses this term to express his intense wish that Job be tested to the end, as if he were undergoing an unending judgment. It is a context of controversy tinged with exasperation: Eliphaz wishes for Job to be continually tested because he considers that his responses resemble those of the wicked. The rare and intense use of this word underscores Eliphaz's passion for judgment.
H0015.portee: This word reminds us that the human heart is capable of deep and sometimes troubling wishes. Here, Eliphaz's desire to see Job tested reveals how moral impatience can become harshness. For the reader, it serves as a warning: our ardent wishes can lead us astray if we do not submit them to God's wisdom.

sens: Aquatic plant with hollow, flexible stems, growing in marshes and shallow waters
Soft material derived from this plant, used to make objects
Light boat or vessel made of woven rushes
H0016.detail: 1. The rush is a plant that grows in water and marshy areas, with hollow and flexible stems. In ancient Egypt and the Near East, it was a common plant along the Nile and lakes. 2. This plant provided a very useful raw material: it was used to make ropes, mats, and various supplies useful for daily life. 3. But its most remarkable use was in the construction of light boats and vessels. These woven rush boats were fast and maneuverable: Job 9:26 compares the speed of Job's days to that of "rush boats" gliding on the water, an image of unparalleled swiftness. These boats were so light and quick that they became the very symbol of fleeting speed.
H0016.origine: The Hebrew word אֵבֶה comes from a root that evokes flexibility and pliability. It specifically designates the rush or papyrus, this aquatic plant well known to the ancient peoples of the Mediterranean and the Near East. The term is related to words meaning "to weave" or "to intertwine," highlighting the primary use of this material: weaving the stems to make useful objects or vessels.
H0016.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 9:26. In this passage, Job, confronted with his sufferings and the swift passage of his life, asserts that his days pass as quickly as the rush boats that sail on the water. This powerful image exploits the ancient reputation of rush boats: light, fast, almost ephemeral, they embody speed and fragility. Job uses them to express the urgency and fleeting nature of human existence in the face of suffering.
H0016.portee: This image of the rush boat speeding across the water invites the reader to meditate on the brevity of life and the rapid passage of time. It reminds us that our days are numbered and fragile, and it prompts awareness of the importance of living well the time that is given to us. In the face of trials like those of Job, this swiftness of time also calls us to turn to the one who alone is eternal.

sens: Exclamation of affliction or regret
Complaint about an unfortunate situation
Expression of compassion or pain
Call to draw attention to distress
H0017.detail:
1. This word is an interjection, meaning a spontaneous exclamation that bursts forth from the lips in response to strong emotion. The biblical "alas" expresses sorrow, regret, or suffering — it is akin to a cry from the heart. In Proverbs 23:29, the drunkard is surrounded by "alas," symbols of misfortunes and complaints that assail him: he suffers from wounds, redness of eyes, and disputes.
2. This exclamation can also express concern, a deep discomfort in the face of what is visible or approaching. It manifests the speaker's desire for things to be different — it is a cry against injustice or distress.
H0017.origine: This word belongs to the family of Hebrew interjections that express intense emotional states. Hebrew uses several exclamations (ah, alas, hey) to convey spontaneous reactions of the heart. The word appears rarely in the Old Testament, reflecting moments when pain or regret is verbalized directly.
H0017.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 23:29. In this verse, the author accumulates the exclamations "alas" to paint the sordid picture of the man given to drunkenness: he is surrounded by misfortunes, quarrels, and wounds. The interjection here serves to express the accumulation of regrets and pains that follow intemperance. It is a generalized complaint about the consequences of debauchery.
H0017.portee: This verse teaches the Christian reader that excessive alcohol produces a cascade of suffering — not mystical punishments, but tangible realities: disputes, wounds, remorse. The "alas" reminds us that each sin brings its own natural consequences. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize how intemperance empties existence of peace and fills it with complaints.

sens: Container or trough where farm animals' food is placed
Place where animals graze, stable or barn
Figurative sense: the relationship between an animal and its master, the attachment to the one who feeds
H0018.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the trough or bin in which hay and oats are placed for the animals: it is a simple and concrete piece of rural life. Isaiah 1:3 mentions it when it says that the donkey knows "the manger of its master" — the animal recognizes the place where it is fed.
2. By extension, the manger represents the stable itself, the home of domestic animals. Proverbs 14:4 plays on this image: "Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty" — without animals to feed, there is nothing to put in the trough, and thus the stable is deserted.
3. Figuratively, the manger symbolizes dependence and attachment: one who eats at the manger acknowledges the one who feeds them. Job 39:12 questions: will the buffalo accept to serve man and spend the night near its manger? It is an image of voluntary submission.
H0018.origine: The Hebrew word אֵבוּס comes from a root that expresses the idea of eating or grazing. The word literally designates the place where one eats — the trough or stable — so that the image is very concrete: what nourishes becomes the symbol of the one who possesses and maintains.
H0018.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, always in relation to farm animals and agrarian life. In all cases, it refers to a context of ownership and care for the animals: it is the sign of the bond between the owner and his flock. In the prophet Isaiah, the manger becomes an image of recognition — the donkey knows its master because he feeds it — to contrast with Israel's ingratitude towards God. In Proverbs, it illustrates the prosperity linked to the possession of livestock. In Job, it symbolizes the place where the creature's submission is fulfilled.
H0018.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on gratitude towards the one who sustains us. The image of the animal recognizing its master at the manger speaks to Christians of the gratitude we owe to God who provides for our needs. It is also an image of care: God is the one who prepares food, who welcomes and nourishes His people as one feeds animals — an image of intimacy and solicitude.

sens: To scare by brandishing a weapon or announcing danger
To brandish the sword at someone as a sign of threat
H0019.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of frightening someone by raising a sword before them, showing that one is ready to strike. It is a threat that is read in the gesture, the raised weapon: the one who brandishes their sword "threatens" their enemies. In Ezekiel 21:20, the Lord says He will threaten the sword against the gates of Jerusalem — that is, He will raise His judgment against the city, visible like a blade that glimmers and is ready to strike down its enemies.
2. In a broader sense, it is to impose a clearly visible threat on someone, to communicate through gestures or words that destruction is near — here, the destruction that the sword of divine judgment will bring.
H0019.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of brandishing and threatening — to scare by exhibiting force. In Ezekiel, it is situated in a context of judgment: God raises His sword against Jerusalem not only to strike but to "threaten," that is, to manifest the reality of the judgment that is coming.
H0019.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 21:20. It is a prophetic word where God announces the siege of Jerusalem: His sword, sharpened and glimmering, threatens the gates of the city. The translation as "threaten" captures the active and dramatic sense well: it is not merely that the sword exists or approaches — it threatens, it brandishes its terrible presence to instill fear in the hearts of the besieged.
H0019.portee: This passage reminds us that God's judgment is not secret or insidious: it is announced, visible, manifest. The threat precedes the blow — it is a call to repentance. To see the sword raised of divine judgment is to have the opportunity to turn to God before it is too late.

sens: juicy fruit with succulent flesh, cultivated especially in ancient Egypt
H0020.detail: 1. The melon is a large fruit with a thick skin and sweet flesh, highly valued in Mediterranean and Eastern regions. The Israelites who left Egypt nostalgically remember the melons they ate there, alongside fish and vegetables (Numbers 11:5): it was familiar and gratifying food, a symbol of the food abundance of the land.
H0020.origine: The Hebrew word אֲבַטִּחִים (avor-tichim) is borrowed from Egyptian vocabulary or ancient Near Eastern languages, reflecting the Egyptian origin of the fruit. The melon did not grow in Israel as it did in Egypt, and the Hebrew word is linked to that exotic and distant world.
H0020.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 11:5. In this context, Israel grumbles in the desert against the manna sent by God, longing for the food pleasures of Egypt. The melon figures among the fruits and vegetables that symbolize this lost abundance, contrasting with the survival food of the desert.
H0020.portee: This verse reminds the believer of the fragility of gratitude: after escaping Egyptian slavery through a miracle, the people regret the comforts of the past rather than trusting in divine provision. The melon here represents the temptation to prefer the comfortable and familiar over God's call, even when He provides for all needs.

sens: Wife of King Ahaz and mother of King Hezekiah
H0021.detail: Abi is the mother of King Hezekiah, one of the most important kings of Judah. She was the daughter of Zechariah and the wife of King Ahaz. The Bible mentions her during the presentation of Hezekiah as king: "His mother was named Abi, daughter of Zechariah" (2 Kings 18:2). She is also referred to as Abijah in the book of Chronicles (2 Chronicles 29:1), both names being a variant of the same Hebrew word.
H0021.origine: The name Abi (אֲבִי) literally means "my father" in Hebrew. In the biblical tradition of feminine names, this type of short name could be given to daughters and women. Her fuller name, Abijah, adds the suffix -yah (יָה) which means "God." She is a woman from the period of the divided kingdom, around the 8th century B.C.
H0021.emploi: Abi appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 18:2, where she is identified as the mother of King Hezekiah. She is also mentioned under the name Abijah in 2 Chronicles 29:1. These brief genealogical mentions highlight her role as the mother of a great reforming king of Judah. Although the Bible does not report any specific actions of Abi, her presence in the text marks the importance of the royal lineage and the succession to the throne of Judah.

sens: Grandfather of Saul, man of the tribe of Benjamin
H0022G.detail: Abiel is a man from the people of Benjamin who lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He is first mentioned in 1 Samuel 9:1 as the grandfather of Saul, the first king of Israel: Saul was the son of Kish, who was the son of Abiel. His name means "God is my father" in Hebrew. Abiel had several children, including Kish (father of Saul) and Ner (father of Abner, the commander of Saul's army), indicating that his descendants played an important role in the history of Israel.
H0022G.origine: The name Abiel literally means "El (God) is (my) father," composed of "ab" (father) and "El" (God). It is a typical theophoric name in biblical Hebrew, where a person's name expressed a confession of faith or a relationship with God.
H0022G.emploi: Abiel appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in the genealogical context of Saul. In 1 Samuel 9:1, he is presented as the grandfather of Saul in the genealogy: Abiel was the father of Kish, who was the father of Saul. In 1 Samuel 14:51, he is mentioned again: "Kish, the father of Saul, and Ner, the father of Abner, were sons of Abiel." This second passage shows that Kish and Ner were brothers, both sons of Abiel. In Chronicles (9:35), Abiel is also called Jeiel.

sens: Warrior who served during the united monarchy in Israel
H0022H.detail: Abiel is one of David's warriors, listed among the royal officers. He is mentioned only once in the Bible: in 1 Chronicles 11:32, among the mighty men who formed the guard and military leaders of the king.
H0022H.origine: The name Abiel means "El (God) is my father" — a composition of the word "abi" (father) and the divine name "El" (God). This type of theophoric name, where the name of God is included, was common in Israel and expressed a relationship of trust in the Lord. Abiel is also known as the grandfather of King Saul, which shows the antiquity and importance of this family lineage.
H0022H.emploi: Abiel appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 11:32, where he is designated as one of the "mighty men" (elite warriors) in the service of King David. He is presented without any other personal details, simply as a warrior who marked the time of the united monarchy.

sens: Levite from the family of Korah
son of Korah and brother of Assir and Elkana
father of Assir and Korah
H0023.detail:
1. Abiasaph is a Levite, a descendant of the tribe of Levi, who lived at the time of the Exodus from Egypt and the sojourn in the desert. His name means "my father has gathered," highlighting divine intervention in the formation of his family.

2. He is the son of Korah, an important figure from the tribe of Levi. Abiasaph has brothers Assir and Elkana, all three sons of the same father (Exodus 6:24).

3. Abiasaph himself becomes the father of two children: Assir and Korah, thus passing on the lineage in the Levitical genealogy.
H0023.origine: The name Abiasaph comes from Hebrew and literally means "my father has gathered" (from "father" and the verb "to gather"). This name testifies to a divine action: the gathering of the family by God's providence. Abiasaph is also called Ebiasaph in some texts, both forms being equivalent. Descendants of Abiasaph appear in later Levitical genealogies, notably in the Chronicles records that mention Asaph, another name associated with this lineage.
H0023.emploi: Abiasaph is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Exodus 6:24, in the context of the genealogies of the Levitical families established at the time of the Exodus from Egypt. The passage lists the sons of Korah and the ancestors of the Korahites, an important branch of Levitical service in the sanctuary. This genealogical catalog establishes the order of succession and the importance of this family among the temple servants.

sens: Young grain of cereal in formation, particularly barley
Month of the Hebrew calendar corresponding to March-April, time of harvest and Passover
H0024.detail:
1. The ear is the part of the cereal that bears the grains: it is the young grain in the process of maturation, particularly barley in the spring. In Exodus 9:31, the barley is struck by hail because it is "in ears" and in bloom — the word thus designates the stage of growth of the grain. In Leviticus 2:14, offerings to God are made of "new ears, roasted in the fire," as firstfruits, meaning the first fruits of the harvest.
2. Abib is also the name of the month when the ears reach maturity in Egypt and Canaan (March or April). It is the first month of the religious Hebrew calendar, the month of the Exodus from Egypt and the Passover. Exodus 13:4 commands: "You are going out today, in the month of the ears," and Deuteronomy 16:1 repeats: "Observe the month of the ears, and celebrate the Passover in honor of the Lord your God; for it is in the month of the ears that the Lord your God brought you out of Egypt." This month would later be called Nisan.
H0024.origine: The Hebrew word אָבִיב (aviv) literally means "young grain" or "tender green." It comes from a root that evokes the growth and youth of wheat and barley in the spring. It is a concrete and agricultural word: it paints the image of the nascent harvest, the moment when the fields are covered with golden ears. This name of the month was replaced after the exile by Nisan, of Akkadian origin, but the Hebrew Bible retains aviv as a poetic and historical term to designate this time of renewal and liberation.
H0024.emploi: Aviv appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in connection with the Exodus and the Passover. In Exodus, the word first designates the physical state of the grain struck by the plagues (Exodus 9:31), then it becomes the name of the month of deliverance (Exodus 13:4, 23:15, 34:18). In Leviticus 2:14, it describes the green ears offered as firstfruits. In Deuteronomy 16:1, it is mentioned as the month of the Passover and the Exodus from Egypt. The word remains always linked to the idea of novelty, growth, and divine liberation.
H0024.portee: Aviv reminds the believer that the Passover and the deliverance from Egypt occur in spring, at the time when nature is renewed and the ears grow. It is a symbol of resurrection and new life: the people come out of slavery as the grain comes out of the ground for the harvest. This connection between nature and salvation teaches that God acts in history according to a sacred rhythm, linked to the cycle of creation. For the Christian, aviv evokes spiritual renewal and the promise that God frees His people from sin, just as He freed them from Egypt.

sens: Wife of Nabal, later wife of David
Intelligent and beautiful woman who intervened to prevent David from committing murder
Mother of Chileab, son of David
H0026G.detail:
1. Abigail is a woman from the time of the united monarchy in Israel, initially married to Nabal, a wealthy but harsh and wicked man (1 Samuel 25:3). She later appears as one of David's wives, whom he took as a wife after Nabal's death (1 Samuel 25:39-42).

2. She is distinguished by her intelligence and beauty: the text describes her as "a woman of good understanding and beautiful appearance" (1 Samuel 25:3). When David, offended by Nabal, prepares to kill him, Abigail discreetly intervenes by bringing him generous provisions and speaking to him with wisdom and respect, which diverts him from his vengeance (1 Samuel 25:18, 32).

3. She becomes the mother of Chileab, one of David's sons, and remains one of his faithful wives, accompanying him during his travels (1 Samuel 30:5; 2 Samuel 3:3).
H0026G.origine: The name means "my father is joy" in Hebrew: it expresses the idea that God, the Father, is the source of joy. This name reflects a trust in divine benevolence. Abigail truly lives up to her name through her wisdom and serenity in difficult moments.
H0026G.emploi: Abigail appears 14 times in the Bible, primarily in 1 Samuel 25, during the confrontation between her, her husband Nabal, and David. She is later mentioned among David's wives during his flights (1 Samuel 27:3), during the captivity at Ziklag (1 Samuel 30:5), and of his sons born in Hebron (2 Samuel 3:3; 1 Chronicles 3:1). Her story, concentrated in a few chapters, is rich: it reveals a courageous, diplomatic, and faithful woman, capable of protecting her household through words and accepting a new love without rebellion.
H0026G.portee: Abigail shows how wisdom and quiet courage can disarm anger and divert from evil. She also illustrates that intelligent women, even in difficult situations (married to an unworthy man), maintain their dignity and can be agents of justice. Her choice to follow David demonstrates a trust in God and in the future beyond present circumstances.

sens: Sister of David and Zeruiah
Mother of Amasa, commander of Absalom's army
H0026H.detail:
1. Abigail is the sister of David, mentioned in the genealogy of the royal family of Israel during the time of the Ark. She is also the sister of Zeruiah, mother of the three renowned warriors Joab, Abishai, and Asahel (1 Chronicles 2:16).
2. She is the wife of Jether the Ishmaelite and the mother of Amasa, who was appointed to lead the army by Absalom during his revolt against David (2 Samuel 17:25; 1 Chronicles 2:17).
H0026H.origine: The name means "my father is joy" in Hebrew. It is a composition of the word "father" and an element expressing joy or exultation. This type of theophoric name was common in the Israelite royal family to express the relationship to God or trust in His goodness.
H0026H.emploi: Abigail appears three times in the Bible, all in the genealogical contexts of the books of Samuel and Chronicles. She is identified as one of the children of Nahash (or mentioned as David's sister according to parallel genealogies) and is part of this remarkable sibling group that included the greatest warriors of Israel. Through her union with Jether, she connects David's family to the Ishmaelites. Her main role in the biblical narrative is to be the mother of Amasa, whose appointment by Absalom represents an attempt to weaken David's power.
H0026H.portee: Abigail illustrates how women in royal times played a decisive role in ensuring dynastic and political continuity, even if they appear only briefly in biblical accounts. Her existence also reminds us that the royal genealogy of Israel was part of broad alliances, notably with neighboring peoples like the Ishmaelites.

sens: Prince of the tribe of Benjamin during the time in the desert
Designated chief to represent Benjamin during the census and offerings at Sinai
H0027.detail: Abidan is a tribal chief, son of Gideoni, chosen to lead the sons of Benjamin during the organization of the people of Israel in the desert. He first appears in the census of Numbers 1:11, where Moses establishes the princes of each tribe. He then presides over all public acts of Benjamin: he organizes the camp (Numbers 2:22), presents offerings during the dedication of Sinai (Numbers 7:60, 7:65), and commands the march of the Benjamite army toward Canaan (Numbers 10:24). His name means "my father is judge," reflecting the judicial and administrative authority that a prince holds in Israel.
H0027.origine: The name Abidan is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Abi" (my father) and "dan" (to judge). It expresses the idea that God is the true judge and the father of the chief; the prince is merely His representative. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, proclaiming a religious conviction.
H0027.emploi: Abidan is mentioned five times, all passages coming from the book of Numbers and covering events at Sinai (around 1445 BC). He is first named during the census of the tribes under Moses' leadership (Numbers 1:11). He is then found each time the sons of Benjamin perform a public act: organizing the camp around the tabernacle (Numbers 2:22), presenting community offerings during the consecration (Numbers 7:60-65), and departing to the desert in good order (Numbers 10:24). These repetitions show that Abidan was a recognized and responsible man, worthy of representing his tribe.
H0027.portee: The figure of Abidan reminds us that God entrusts certain individuals with the care of governing and serving the people according to His justice. It also shows how the Church functions: each community leader must act as a representative of the one who truly judges. The name itself invites us to recognize that all legitimate human authority comes from God, whose justice remains.

sens: Son of Midian and grandson of Abraham
One of the five sons of Keturah, Abraham's second wife
H0028.detail: Abida is one of the sons that Midian had. Midian himself was the son of Abraham and his second wife Keturah, after the death of Sarah. Abida is mentioned alongside his brothers Epha, Epher, Henoch, and Eldaa in the genealogy of Abraham's descendants.
H0028.origine: The name Abida means "my father knows" in ancient Hebrew (from ab, "father," and yada, "to know"). It is a theophoric name, meaning it acknowledges a relationship with God, the Father who knows all things.
H0028.emploi: Abida appears twice in the Bible, always in genealogical lists. He first appears in Genesis 25:4, at the time when the narrative enumerates the children of Keturah after Abraham's death. The same genealogy is repeated in 1 Chronicles 1:33. These two passages provide no details about his personal life, only his place in Abraham's family tree and his descendants.

sens: Son of the prophet Samuel, judge in Israel during the time of the united monarchy
H0029G.detail: Abijah is the second son of the prophet Samuel. He is mentioned as a judge at Beer-Sheba alongside his older brother Joel (1 Samuel 8:2). His existence is also attested in the genealogy of the Levites (1 Chronicles 6:28), where he is named among Samuel's descendants.
H0029G.origine: The name Abijah means "Jehovah is my father" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: "Abi" (father) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah). This type of theophoric name, where the divine name appears, was common in Israel to express the child's relationship to God or the prayer of the parents.
H0029G.emploi: Abijah appears twice in the Old Testament. He is first mentioned in 1 Samuel 8:2 as one of Samuel's two sons who judged at Beer-Sheba. The second mention, in 1 Chronicles 6:28, places him in the list of Samuel's sons as a Levite. These brief mentions provide no details about his actions or character but inscribe him in the lineage of the great prophet Samuel.

sens: son of Jeroboam, king of Israel during the divided monarchy
H0029H.detail: Abijah is the son of Jeroboam I, the king who separated the kingdom of Israel from that of Judah. He appears in the account of 1 Kings 14:1, where he falls ill. His name means "Jehovah is (my) father," an affirmation of trust in God despite the troubled political situation of the Northern kingdom. The biblical text mentions him little, but his existence shows how the ordinary lives of those close to the king intersected with the great events of Israel's history.
H0029H.origine: The name Abijah is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Abi" (father) and "Yah" (an abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah). It therefore means "Jehovah is my father." It is a theophoric name, common in Israel, which expresses familial piety and the confession that God is the true father and protector of the people.
H0029H.emploi: Abijah is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 14:1. He is the son of Jeroboam I, king of the Northern kingdom (Israel), who reigned after the division of the monarchy (around 922 B.C.). The biblical text shows him ill, which prompts his mother to approach the prophet Ahijah to learn the fate of the young child. Although not developed in the narrative, this passage illustrates how even the children of great kings were subjected to trials and the will of God.

sens: King of Judah, son and successor of Rehoboam
Victorious warrior against Jeroboam and Israel of the North
H0029I.detail:
1. Abijah is a king of Judah who reigns after his father Rehoboam. He is mentioned as early as 1 Chronicles 3:10 in the genealogy of the kings of Judah, and his reign begins in the 18th year of King Jeroboam of Israel (2 Chronicles 13:1). Rehoboam even established him in the first rank among his brothers to make him king (2 Chronicles 11:22).
2. Abijah is best known for his decisive military victory against Jeroboam and the Northern kingdom of Israel. Although Jeroboam has an army twice as numerous (800,000 warriors against 400,000), Abijah wins the victory: the Lord strikes Israel before him and Judah (2 Chronicles 13:15), then he pursues Jeroboam, taking several cities like Bethel and Jeshanah (2 Chronicles 13:19), and kills 500,000 elite men (2 Chronicles 13:17).
H0029I.origine: The name means "Jehovah is (my) father," composed of the Hebrew word for father (Abi) and the divine name (Yah). It is a theophoric name, common in the Bible, which expresses spiritual filiation and divine protection of the bearer. The same character is also called Abijam in the Kings.
H0029I.emploi: Abijah appears 15 times in the Chronicles, concentrated mainly in chapter 13 of 2 Chronicles which recounts his glorious victory. The usages describe him as the son of Rehoboam and Maacah (2 Chronicles 11:20-22), as a king anointed by God to reign over Judah (2 Chronicles 13:1-2), and as a victorious military leader whose success comes from the Lord. He dies after his reign and is succeeded by his son Asa (2 Chronicles 13:23; 14:1). The texts of the Chronicles present Abijah as a warrior king whose success rests on divine favor, in contrast to the less favorable portrait in the book of Kings.
H0029I.portee: Abijah illustrates how God supports a king who relies on Him, even in the face of overwhelming numerical superiority. His example shows that victories are not won by military might alone, but by trust in God and obedience to His will. For the believer, it is an encouragement: seemingly insurmountable challenges are never without a way out when one relies on the Lord.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Judah during the time of Egypt and the desert
Wife of Hezron
Mother of Ashhur
H0029J.detail:
1. Abijah is a woman belonging to the tribe of Judah, living during the events of Egypt and the desert. She appears only in genealogies, which shows that she has a role in the history of the chosen people, even if few details are given about her life.
2. She was the wife of Hezron, a man from the genealogy of Judah. The marriage was important for establishing the lines of descent that would later form the tribes and families of Israel.
3. She is best known as the mother of Ashhur, to whom the text gives the title of "father of Tekoa," indicating that he founded a city or region and that his descendants settled there. It is through her motherhood that Abijah fits into the genealogical chain that traverses the history of Israel.
H0029J.origine: The name Abijah (or Abia, Abiah, Abijah) means "Jehovah is (my) father." It is composed of two elements: "Ab" which means father, and an element that refers to the divine name. This name expresses a trust or proclamation: the one who bears it affirms that God is his father, that is, his protection and support. The same name has been borne by several other characters in the history of Israel (kings, priests, sons of prophets), showing its common character and pious significance.
H0029J.emploi: Abijah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:24. She is mentioned there as the wife of Hezron and the mother of Ashhur. This passage is part of the genealogy of Judah, one of the twelve tribes. These genealogies in the Book of Chronicles aimed to remind the Israelites who returned from exile of the continuity of their people and the legitimacy of their family lines. Although not detailed, the mention of Abijah shows that women had a place in these genealogical records, as mothers and transmitters of the family name.
H0029J.portee: Abijah reminds readers that the genealogy of God's people was built by women as well as by men. Her appearance in the Chronicles testifies that God does not despise the ordinary history of believers, even the most humble. It invites us to see how each person, known or unknown, fits into God's plan for His people.

sens: Son of Becher, of the tribe of Benjamin
H0029K.detail: 1. Abijah is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogies of Israel. He is one of the nine sons of Becher, listed in 1 Chronicles 7:8 among the descendants of this Benjaminite branch. Nothing more is known about his life or actions; he appears only in this genealogical list.
H0029K.origine: The name Abijah means "God (Jehovah) is my father" in Hebrew: "abi" means father, and "ja" is a divine abbreviation. This theophoric name (that is, containing the name of God) was common in Israel and borne by several important characters, including a king of Judah and a son of the prophet Samuel, but this one is simply a man of the tribe of Benjamin whose name has only survived.
H0029K.emploi: Abijah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:8, as one of the sons of Becher. This mention is part of a genealogical series that enumerates the descendants of Benjamin. No other details about his life, deeds, or role are provided by Scripture.

sens: Chief of a Levitical priestly house
H0029L.detail: 1. Abijah refers to the chief of one of the twenty-four priestly houses established by David to organize the service of the Levites at the temple. In 1 Chronicles 24:10, he is mentioned as the head of the eighth house in the order of the drawing of lots that determined the calendar of sacrifices and ceremonies.
H0029L.origine: The name Abijah means "Jehovah is (my) father" in Hebrew: it combines the word "father" with the divine name. It is a classic theophoric name in Israel, borne by several important characters in biblical history: a king of Judah, a son of the prophet Samuel, and other royal and priestly figures. The priestly house of Abijah continued to be important even after the Babylonian exile.
H0029L.emploi: The mention of Abijah in 1 Chronicles 24:10 identifies him as one of the heads of the twenty-four priestly divisions established during the organization of worship at the temple in Jerusalem. His name appears in the official list that governed the rotational service of the Levitical priests. This organization was fundamental to ensure the continuity of worship and the equitable distribution of priestly service among the different families of priests.

sens: Chief of a priestly house at the time of the return from exile
H0029M.detail: 1. Abijah is the name of a chief of a priestly house (that is, a group of priests and Levites) who lived after the return from exile in Babylon. His name appears in the official lists of those who signed the covenant during the reconstruction of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 10:7), which shows his importance in the restored religious community.
H0029M.origine: The name Abijah (אֲבִיָּה) means "Jehovah is (my) father": it is composed of two Hebrew elements, ab (father) and Yah (an abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah). It is a theophoric name, very common in the Bible, which expresses a confession of faith: recognizing God as father. The same name was borne by several important figures in the history of Israel: notably a king of Judah (son of Rehoboam) and a son of the prophet Samuel.
H0029M.emploi: The Abijah mentioned in the three provided instances is a priestly chief during the return from exile under Zerubbabel and Ezra (after 538 B.C.). He is listed in Nehemiah 10:7 among the signers of God's covenant, alongside other religious and civil leaders who committed to obey the Law. His name reappears in Nehemiah 12:4 and 12:17, in the records of the heads of priestly houses of that time, who served in an organized manner at the restored Temple. These three references designate the same character or his direct successor in the role.

sens: Mother of King Hezekiah of Judah
H0029N.detail: Abijah is the mother of King Hezekiah, who reigned in Jerusalem in the 8th century B.C. She was the daughter of Zechariah and the wife of King Ahaz. She appears in the biblical account as the mother of a king who made significant religious reforms in Judah (2 Chronicles 29:1).
H0029N.origine: The name Abijah means "Jehovah is (my) father." It is composed of the divine name "Jehovah" and the word "father," expressing a relationship of trust toward God. This type of theophoric name was common among the royal families of Israel and Judah, reflecting the acknowledgment of divine sovereignty.
H0029N.emploi: Abijah is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 29:1, where she is identified as the mother of Hezekiah. She appears in the genealogy of the king, which underscores the importance of her role in the royal lineage of Judah. Her appearance in the biblical text establishes her place in the dynastic history of Judah, during a period marked by the religious reforms of Hezekiah.

sens: Son of Aaron and Elisheba
Brother of Nadab, Eleazar, and Ithamar
Levitical priest during the wilderness period
Offering strange fire before the Lord
H0030.detail: Abihu is one of the four sons of Aaron, the first high priest of Israel. Along with his brothers Nadab, Eleazar, and Ithamar, he is part of the first generation of priests of the Lord, chosen to serve at the Tabernacle (Exodus 6:23; Exodus 24:9). However, Nadab and Abihu commit a grave act: they bring strange fire before the Lord, that is, fire that He had not commanded them to offer (Leviticus 10:1). This act, although it is unclear what motivated it—pride, impatience, or simple disobedience—violates the order established by God for worship. The Lord immediately punishes this transgression: Nadab and Abihu perish before Him in the wilderness of Sinai (Numbers 3:4). Only Eleazar and Ithamar survive and continue the priestly service under the authority of their father Aaron.
H0030.origine: The name Abihu literally means "he is (my) father," from the Hebrew word "abi" (father) and the pronoun "hu" (he). It is a theophoric name, expressing a filial relationship, probably toward God or an affirmation of faith. The name reflects the religious convictions of the priestly family.
H0030.emploi: Abihu appears twelve times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers, which cover the Sinai and wilderness period. He is always mentioned with his brothers, particularly with Nadab, his twin brother or very close in age. The two major accounts concerning him are on the one hand his designation as a priest (Exodus 6:23; Exodus 24:9), and on the other hand his death due to strange fire (Leviticus 10:1; Numbers 3:4; Numbers 26:61). The parallel between his initial integration into the priesthood and his swift death highlights the critical importance of exact obedience in divine worship.
H0030.portee: The story of Abihu teaches a serious lesson: worshiping God requires precise obedience and respect for divine directives. It is not enough to be consecrated or well-intentioned; disobedience, even if unintentional, carries consequences. For the believer, this account serves as a reminder that the fear of God and careful listening to His Word are the foundations of service that is pleasing to Him.

sens: Benjamite during the time of Egypt and the wilderness, son of Bela
H0031.detail: Abihud is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:3, where he is listed among the sons of Bela. His name literally means "my father is majesty" or "my father is greatness." He lived during the time of Egypt and the wilderness, that is, during the patriarchal period or the stay in Egypt.
H0031.origine: The name Abihud is composed of two Hebrew elements: "abi" (אֲבִי) which means "my father," and "hud" which refers to majesty or greatness. It is a theophoric name, that is, a name bearing the name or a quality of God: it expresses the personal relationship of the father with God or proclaims a divine quality in the family context. Many Benjamite names from this period follow this same pattern.
H0031.emploi: Abihud appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:3, in the genealogical list of the tribe of Benjamin. He is cited as one of the sons of Bela, alongside his brothers Addar, Gera, Naaman, Ard, Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, Iri, and Ahoah. This Benjamin genealogy was important for the identity and lineage of the Benjamites after the return from exile.

sens: Levitical man during the time of Moses
Father of the chief Tzuriel
H0032G.detail: 1. Abihaïl is a Levitical man who lived during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness. He is the father of Tzuriel, who himself was the chief of the paternal house of the families of Merari—that is, he led an important group of Levites, those priests responsible for the care of the tabernacle (Numbers 3:35). 2. His name literally means "my father is power," which reflects a trust in the strength and protection of the God of Israel.
H0032G.origine: The name Abihaïl is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Abi" which means "my father" and "Haïl" which means "power" or "strength." It is a typical theophoric name of the Old Testament, which expresses the believer's relationship to God by calling Him "my father." Several people bear this name in Scripture, reflecting its popularity in the history of Israel.
H0032G.emploi: Abihaïl appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 3:35, in the context of the numbering of the Levites in the wilderness. He is mentioned as the father of Tzuriel, the chief of the families of Merari. This unique mention shows that Scripture allows us to know his ancestors: Abihaïl embodies one of the many generations of Levites who served God and participated in the sacred organization of the people of Israel at the time of the Exodus.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
Wife of Abishur and mother of Ahban and Molid
H0032H.detail:
1. Abichail is a woman of the tribe of Judah who lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. She appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Judah recorded in the registers of Israel.
2. She is the wife of Abishur and the mother of two sons: Ahban and Molid. Her name appears in 1 Chronicles 2:29 in a genealogical list, where she is simply referred to as "the wife of Abishur" who "bore him Ahban and Molid."
H0032H.origine: The name Abichail literally means "my father is mighty" or "my father is strength" in Hebrew: "abi" (father) and "chail" (might, strength, vigor). It is a name of faith confession, expressing recognition of the power of the divine father. This name was borne by several individuals in the Old Testament, but this entry concerns only the woman mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2:29.
H0032H.emploi: Abichail is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:29. She is listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, among the descendants of Jerahmeel. Her role is limited to her identity as a wife and mother: she is identified by her relationship to Abishur and by her children Ahban and Molid. No particular event or detail of her life is reported; she represents a link in the genealogical chain of God's people.

sens: man of the tribe of Gad during the time of the divided monarchy of Israel
H0032I.detail: This name designates a man of the tribe of Gad, appearing in the genealogy of the descendants of Gad at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between North and South (1 Chronicles 5:14). He is presented as the son of Huri and the father of several children including Michael, Meshullam, and others.
H0032I.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "my father is strength" or "my father is might": it expresses the confidence that the Lord is the strength and protection of the bearer of the name. It is a theophoric name, meaning it includes a reference to God (father) as the source of strength.
H0032I.emploi: This name appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 5:14, in the genealogy of the tribe of Gad. He is an ordinary man of this tribe whose name is preserved in the Bible only because he is part of the genealogical chain of Gad, one of the twelve tribes of Israel.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
H0032J.detail: Abichail is a Jewish woman from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. She is the daughter of Eliab, son of Jesse, and becomes the wife of King Rehoboam. She is the mother of Mahalath, who will marry Jerimoth, son of King David. Her name, which means "my father is strength" or "my father is might", emphasizes the importance of paternal lineage in biblical genealogies. She appears only once in the Scriptures, in 2 Chronicles 11:18, where she is mentioned as part of the royal wives of King Rehoboam.
H0032J.origine: The name Abichail is composed of two Hebrew elements: "abi" (אֲבִי) meaning "my father" and "hayil" (חַיִל) meaning "strength", "might", or "valor". It is a theophoric name that expresses the relationship of the child to their father and affirms that the father possesses strength. The same name appears for several other individuals in the Old Testament, including a Levite during the time of Moses, a Gadite, and the father of Esther.
H0032J.emploi: Abichail appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 11:18. She is presented as the daughter of Eliab, son of Jesse (which would make her a close relative of King David), and as the wife of King Rehoboam of Judah.
