Through her marriage to the king, she enters the royal family and becomes the mother of Mahalath. This mention is part of the genealogy of the royal families of Judah at the time of the division of the kingdom.

sens: Uncle of Mordecai and adoptive father of Esther
Man of the Jewish royal family during the exile in Babylon
H0032K.detail: 1. Abichail is the adoptive father of Esther, the queen who will become the wife of King Ahasuerus. He is the one who raised Esther after she lost her parents, as her uncle. When Esther is brought to the royal palace to be presented to the king, she is referred to as his daughter (Esther 2:15). 2. Abichail lives during the time of the exile of the Jews in Babylon, when Israel is under Persian rule. He appears as an influential man in the Jewish community, as his relative Mordecai holds an important position at the royal court and Esther becomes queen (Esther 9:29).
H0032K.origine: The name Abichail means "my father is strength" or "my father is might". It is composed of two Hebrew roots: "abi" (my father) and "chail" (might, strength, dignity). It is a theophoric name, meaning it expresses a confession of faith by relating God ("my father") to a divine quality. Several men and women bear this name in the Bible, reflecting its importance in Jewish tradition.
H0032K.emploi: Abichail appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Esther, where he is presented as the father of Esther. He is a Jewish character living in exile in Babylon under the reign of Ahasuerus. His role in the biblical story is to serve as a family link: he took in and raised Esther, allowing this orphaned young girl to become queen and save her people from extermination. Although Abichail himself is not an actor in the dramatic events of the book, his presence reminds us of familial faithfulness and the divine Providence that protects the Jewish people.
H0032K.portee: The figure of Abichail illustrates the invisible yet crucial role of adoptive parents and educators in God's plan. His love for Esther and his commitment to protect her pave the way for the miraculous deliverance of the entire Jewish people. For the Christian reader, Abichail reminds us that God often uses ordinary human relationships and daily acts of faithfulness to accomplish His plan of salvation.

sens: descendant d'Abiezer, homme de la tribu de Manassé
membre de la famille d'Abiezer
originaire du clan d'Abiezer
H0033.detail: 1. Abiezer is primarily the name of an ancestor, a man of the tribe of Manasseh during the time of Egypt and the desert; his name means "my father is my help". 2. The term then designates each of his descendants, all members of his family or clan. In the book of Judges, this is how Gideon is referred to: he belongs to the family of Abiezer (Judges 6:11), which connects him to this prestigious lineage. 3. This family affiliation defines identity and social status: the land at Ophrah "belonged to the family of Abiezer" (Judges 6:24, 8:32), showing that the clan possessed its own lands in the region.
H0033.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "father" and "help" or "support". Abiezer is the son of Gilead, who is the son of Manasseh, the son of Joseph. The name is sometimes shortened to "Jezer". It is a typical patronymic of the Old Testament: it identifies a founding ancestor of a tribe or clan, and all his descendants bear this name as a mark of belonging.
H0033.emploi: The word appears three times in Judges, always in connection with Gideon and his region. In Judges 6:11, Gideon is presented as being from the family of Abiezer. In Judges 6:24 and 8:32, it is the land of Ophrah that is said to "belong" to this family. The three occurrences show how the clan of Abiezer possessed a fixed territory in Israel and how Gideon, one of its members, would become a great deliverer.
H0033.portee: This patronymic reminds us that God works through families and generations. Gideon, although from a modest family, becomes the leader that Israel awaited. This shows that human identity is rooted in familial and territorial ties, and that God chooses His servants not according to their initial status, but according to His grace.

sens: person who lacks what is necessary to live
one who is crushed, oppressed, defenseless
one who suffers and calls for God's help
the poorest, the weakest in society
H0034.detail:
1. The indigent is one who has nothing, who lacks bread and resources. It is the poor in the most raw sense of the term, reduced to begging to survive (Exodus 23:6: the defenseless poor in a trial).
2. It is also one who suffers mistreatment from the powerful, crushed by the wicked who take advantage of his weakness (Psalms 37:14: the sword is drawn against the indigent and the unfortunate).
3. The indigent cries out to God; it is one who needs divine help to escape misery and oppression (Job 5:15: God saves him from the hand of the powerful; Isaiah 41:17: the Lord hears the indigent who cry out from thirst).
4. The word also designates an entire social class, the last, those who have no weight in the community and whom the laws must specially protect (Deuteronomy 15:11: there will always be indigents in the land).
H0034.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes lack, deprivation. Its starting image is that of one who is empty, who has nothing. It is a classic Hebrew word to designate the poor, parallel to other words in the same family that all express absence, emptiness, insufficiency in the face of life's needs.
H0034.emploi: This word appears about 58 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the books of wisdom and the prophets. It is constant in the law (Deuteronomy) where God prescribes protecting the indigent and leaving them portions (Deuteronomy 15:11; Exodus 23:6). The psalms take it up to show that God defends the indigent against his oppressors (Psalms 37:14; 82:4; 140:13). The prophets use it to denounce those who oppress the indigent (Amos 2:6; 4:1; 8:4) and to promise that God will lift him up (Isaiah 41:17). The word can also designate the condition of indigence, the state of misery and dependence.
H0034.portee: The figure of the indigent runs through the Bible as a call to justice and compassion. It reveals that God cares first for those who have nothing, who cannot defend themselves. For the Christian, it is a challenge: to protect the indigent, to refuse to oppress him, is to serve God Himself. It is also an invitation to recognize that we are all, spiritually, indigents before God, dependent on His grace.

sens: Small Mediterranean shrub with edible fruits, used in cooking as a condiment
Appetite or desire stimulant, especially due to its reputed aphrodisiac properties in antiquity
H0035.detail:
1. The caper is a thorny shrub that grows in the warm regions of the Middle East and the Mediterranean basin. Its small, tangy fruits, flower buds, or small berries are preserved in vinegar or brine and serve as a tasty condiment in cooking. The word thus evokes a common culinary product in biblical times.

2. In antiquity, the caper was reputed to stimulate sexual appetite or desire in general. In Ecclesiastes 12:7, the text lists the signs of approaching old age: "the caper no longer has effect," meaning that even this natural stimulant loses its virtue for the tired old man. The word thus designates less the fruit itself than its tonifying and exciting effect.
H0035.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root meaning "to desire" or "to be hungry." It is formed in a way that makes it a concrete noun: that which excites desire, hence "caper." Ancient Hebrew and Greek texts associated this fruit with its stimulating properties on the body and appetite, which explains why the word evokes more the effect than the object.
H0035.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 12:7. The wise man describes the moment when the old man gradually loses his strength and pleasures, including appetite. The reputed stimulant, the caper, thus figures in a poetic list of things that cease to function with age. It is a concrete and savory detail: even tonic condiments no longer sharpen the desire of the old man who is going to his eternal home.
H0035.portee: This passage invites us to meditate on human finitude and the realities of old age, without dramatizing but with lucidity. Recognizing that our bodies and desires change over time is to humbly accept the wisdom of God who governs the seasons of life. It also reminds us that the essential is not in ephemeral pleasures but in preparing for our encounter with the Eternal.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the divided monarchy
H0036.detail: Abithub is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Shaharaim and Huschim, and the brother of several children: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Sachia, Mirmah, and Elpaal (1 Chronicles 8:11). His name literally means "my father is goodness" or "my father is good," expressing gratitude towards God.
H0036.origine: The name Abithub comes from Hebrew and is composed of two elements: "ab" (father) and "tub" (goodness, well). This type of compound name was common in Israel and reflected the faith of the parents in God. The name expresses a conviction that God, as a father, is the source of all good.
H0036.emploi: Abithub appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 8:11, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. He is listed among the descendants of Shaharaim, who is himself a minor character about whom little is known. This genealogical passage is part of the lists that reconstruct the history of Israel after the Babylonian exile. Although little known, Abithub represents the many people of the tribe of Benjamin whose lives contributed to the history of God's people.

sens: Wife of David and mother of Schephathia
One of King David's wives during the time of united Israel
H0037.detail: Abithal is a woman of King David's royal court, living at the time when David ruled over all Israel. She is the mother of Schephathia, who is listed among David's sons in 2 Samuel 3:4 as "the fifth" son born during David's reign in Hebron. Her name appears in the royal lists of the Old Testament that inventory David's sons born of different mothers.
H0037.origine: The name Abithal literally means "my father is the dew." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: "abi" meaning "my father" and "tal" meaning "dew." Dew in biblical thought often symbolizes freshness, life, and divine blessing, so this name expresses a paternal blessing or an invocation of divine protection.
H0037.emploi: Abithal appears twice in the Bible, both times in genealogical lists of David's sons. In 2 Samuel 3:4, she is mentioned as the mother of David's fifth son, Schephathia, born in Hebron. The same information is repeated in 1 Chronicles 3:3, which recaps the sons born to David before his installation in Jerusalem. These two passages are part of the historical enumerations of David's women and his descendants.

sens: King of Judah, son and successor of Rehoboam
Heir prince of the divided kingdom in the 10th century BC
H0038.detail: Abijam is the name of a king of Judah who reigned after his father Rehoboam. He ascended to the throne in the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam, king of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 15:1), and reigned over Judah for about three years. His reign was marked by military tensions: the Bible reports that there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:7). Upon his death, he was buried in the city of David, according to the practice of the kings of Judah (1 Kings 15:8), and his son Asa succeeded him.
H0038.origine: The name Abijam means "my father is the sea" or "Yah is my father." It is a variant or alternative form of the name Abijah (אֲבִיָּה), both referring to the same king of Judah. The name evokes the idea that the father — probably God — is a protection for the bearer, a common image in Hebrew theophoric names.
H0038.emploi: Abijam appears four times in 1 Kings 14-15, all instances drawn from historical accounts of the divided kingdom. The first occurrence (1 Kings 14:31) introduces him as the son of Rehoboam and the new heir to the throne of Judah, after the death of his father. The other three occurrences (1 Kings 15:1, 7, 8) recount his rise to power, his conflict with Jeroboam, and his death. The text presents him as a warrior king of the southern kingdom during the period of instability that followed the political and religious schism of Israel.

sens: Man who lived during the time of the Patriarchs, son of Joktan and descendant of Shem
H0039.detail: Abimaël is a man mentioned in the genealogy of ancient peoples. He is the son of Joktan, who himself descended from Shem, one of Noah's three sons. His name appears twice in the Bible, in two parallel genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:28 and in 1 Chronicles 1:22, where he is listed among the brothers descended from Joktan (Almodad, Ebal, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, Jobab, and others). These genealogies enumerate the ancestors of the peoples who populated the earth after the flood.
H0039.origine: The name Abimaël literally means "my father is El (God)." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: "abi" meaning "my father" and "El" referring to God. This type of theophoric name (i.e., containing the name of God) was common in ancient Near Eastern cultures to express the relationship of the bearer to the deity.
H0039.emploi: Abimaël appears only twice in the Bible, both in genealogical tables: Genesis 10:28 and 1 Chronicles 1:22. These two passages provide the same list of descendants of Joktan, suggesting that Chronicles repeats and confirms the account from Genesis. Abimaël represents one of the families or peoples that settled after the Tower of Babel. Although his name is preserved, no details of his life or deeds are provided by the biblical text.

sens: King of Gerar during the time of Abraham
Philistine king or royal title during the time of David
Son of Gideon born of a concubine
H0040G.detail:
1. Abimelech is first a king of Gerar who encounters Abraham during the time of the Patriarchs. When Abraham presents Sarah as his sister, Abimelech takes her for his harem (Genesis 20:2); but God warns him in a dream that she is married. Abimelech acknowledges his mistake, returns Sarah to Abraham, and gives him livestock and land (Genesis 20:14). Later, he makes a covenant with Abraham at Beersheba (Genesis 21:32).
2. During the time of David, a king or Philistine chief of the same name (or holding the same royal title) reigns at Gath. This suggests that Abimelech may have been a title held by Philistine kings, similar to "Pharaoh" for the Egyptians.
3. An Abimelech is also the son of the judge Gideon and a concubine; he attempts to make himself king of Israel, but this project turns tragic.
H0040G.origine: The name Abimelech means "My father is king" (or perhaps "The king is my father"). It reflects the relationship of a king to his god or a tutelary deity, or the assertion of his royal power. This name could be a dynastic title of Philistine rulers.
H0040G.emploi: Abimelech appears at least three times in Scripture: first as king of Gerar during the time of Abraham (Genesis 20 and 21), then as king of Gath during the time of David (Genesis 26), and finally as the son of Gideon (Judges 8-9). The first two cases may refer to different individuals or the same name/title held by multiple Philistine kings. The story of Abraham shows an Abimelech who is honest and fears God, quick to acknowledge his wrongdoing and restore justice. His covenant with Abraham marks a lasting peace between these two influential men.

sens: Son of Gideon born of a concubine, who proclaimed himself king of Shechem
Warrior who seized power through violence and cunning
Man judged by God for his bloody ambition
H0040H.detail:
1. Abimelech is the illegitimate son of Gideon, born to a servant woman from Shechem. After Gideon's death, he is recognized as king by the inhabitants of Shechem, who choose him over his many legitimate brothers (Judges 9:6).

2. He seizes power through murder: he kills his seventy half-brothers on one stone to eliminate all rivals, with only Jotham escaping (Judges 9:5, 9:18). He then reigns for three years over Shechem, using violence and cunning to maintain his authority.

3. His tragic end illustrates God's judgment: during the siege of Thebez, a woman mortally wounds him by throwing a millstone on his head, and he must ask his armor-bearer to finish him off so that he does not die by a woman (Judges 9:50-55). The Bible concludes that God repaid the evil he had done to his brothers (Judges 9:56).
H0040H.origine: The name means "My father is king" or "Melek is father" (Melek = king, Abi = father). This name perhaps reflects a claim to royal legitimacy despite his illegitimate birth. It is also the title held by the kings of Gerar during the time of Abraham and by Philistine kings, suggesting a lineage or custom of coronation in the ancient world.
H0040H.emploi: Abimelech appears 40 times in the book of Judges, almost entirely in chapter 9, which recounts his story from beginning to end. The narrative shows a ruthless ambitious man: he seduces the Shechemites by presenting himself as one of them (Judges 9:2-3), they proclaim him king (Judges 9:6), then he organizes the massacre of his brothers (Judges 9:4-5). He then fights against the revolts of Shechem against him (Judges 9:34-45), until his final siege against Thebez. The context emphasizes that God himself disrupts the relationships between Abimelech and the Shechemites, sending an evil spirit to stir them against each other (Judges 9:23).
H0040H.portee: The story of Abimelech teaches that tyrannical and murderous ambition leads to ruin, and that God does not leave it unpunished. It also warns that the people who place their hope in a violent leader without justice end up being destroyed. God's judgment is executed through human means — a woman, a millstone — reminding that the Lord overturns the powerful who oppress, and that violence begets violence.

sens: King of Gath during the time of King David
Another name for King Achish of Gath
H0040I.detail:
1. Abimelech is a Philistine king of Gath who lived during the time of King David. Psalm 34 mentions him at a moment when David had to feign madness to escape from his presence (Psalms 34:1).
2. This name Abimelech is another designation for King Achish, the ruler of the Philistine city of Gath. It is possible that "Abimelech" was a title held by Philistine kings rather than a unique personal name, similar to how one might refer to "Pharaoh" in Egypt.
H0040I.origine: The name means "my father is king" or "the king is my father." It combines two Hebrew elements: "Abi" (father) and "Melek" (king). This name reflects a conception of royal power where the sovereign is seen as a paternal figure for his people. Several biblical characters bear this name at different times in Israel's history.
H0040I.emploi: Abimelech is mentioned in Psalm 34 as the king to whom David presented himself while fleeing from Saul. To escape the threat, David pretended to be mad before this Philistine king. This encounter marks a decisive moment in David's life in exile. The fact that Abimelech is also called Achish suggests that this title was used to designate successive kings of Gath during this period.
H0040I.portee: The story of David before Abimelech shows how God protects His servants in times of extreme danger, even far from their land and in the face of Israel's enemies. It teaches the reader that trust in God can take unexpected forms and that God works to save His people through mysterious paths.

sens: Priest during the time of David
Son of the priest Abiathar
H0040J.detail:
1. Abimelech is a priest mentioned during the time of King David, serving at the sanctuary of Israel alongside the priest Zadok. In 1 Chronicles 18:16, he is listed among the royal officials, indicating his importance in the religious administration of the kingdom.

2. He is the son of the priest Abiathar, who was himself a major figure in the priesthood under David and Solomon. This priestly lineage places him among the servants of the worship of the Eternal.
H0040J.origine: The name Abimelech literally means "my father is king" or "the king is my father," formed from two Hebrew words: "abi" (father) and "melek" (king). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries a statement of faith: it expresses that God is the true king and father. This name has been borne by several important characters in Israel's history (a king of Gerar during Abraham's time, a king of Gath during David's time, a son of Gideon), but here it refers to the son of Abiathar.
H0040J.emploi: Abimelech is mentioned only once in the Segond 1910, in 1 Chronicles 18:16, in the list of officers of King David. He is named as a priest (sacrificer) alongside Zadok. This unique appearance, in a text listing the great figures of David's government, indicates that he held a high rank in the religious hierarchy of the kingdom, although the details of his life and ministry are not reported in the biblical text.

sens: Inhabitant of Gibeah who welcomed the Ark of the Covenant into his house
Son of Jesse and older brother of King David
H0041G.detail:
1. Abinadab is first known as the man of Gibeah with whom the people of Kiriath-Jearim transported the Ark of the Covenant after its capture by the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:1). His son Eleazar was consecrated to be its guardian, and the Ark remained with Abinadab for about twenty years. His two other sons, Uzzah and Ahio, drove the cart when the Ark was later moved (2 Samuel 6:3-4).

2. Abinadab also appears as the second son of Jesse and the older brother of David. Although he is mentioned in the family lineage, the Bible reports very few details about his personal life, unlike David who became king.
H0041G.origine: The name Abinadab means "my father is noble" or "my father is generous." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: "abi" (father) and "nadab" (to be generous, to be willing). It is a family name carrying values of nobility and benevolence.
H0041G.emploi: Abinadab appears four times in Holy Scripture. Historically, he is the same man mentioned in 1 Samuel 7:1 and 2 Samuel 6:3-4 (with the parallel in 1 Chronicles 13:7): the one whose house in Gibeah welcomed the Ark of the Covenant after its arrival at Kiriath-Jearim. However, there is theological debate as to whether the Abinadab mentioned as the son of Jesse (in the genealogical lists not transcribed here) is the same person or a namesake. The Bible emphasizes this Abinadab's role as the keeper of the Ark, a symbol of the divine presence.
H0041G.portee: Abinadab illustrates the importance of hospitality towards holy things and faithful service. His house became a place of reverence where the Ark of the Covenant, a symbol of divine presence and covenant, was honored and safeguarded. His example shows that serving God also involves welcoming and protecting the visible signs of His presence.

sens: Son of Saul, king of Israel
Brother of Jonathan and Malchishua
H0041H.detail: Abinadab is one of the sons of King Saul, born of his marriage to Ahinoam. He is the brother of Jonathan, the most famous warrior of Israel, and of Malchishua. Along with his father and brothers, he perished in battle against the Philistines on Mount Gilboa: "The Philistines pursued Saul and his sons, and killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul" (1 Samuel 31:2). This death marks the tragic end of Saul's reign and the rise of David.
H0041H.origine: The name Abinadab means "my father is noble" or "my father is willing" — it expresses the father's willingness. It is a theophoric name (containing the word "Ab" meaning "father") common in ancient Israel. Several characters bear this name: notably a man of Gibeah who welcomed the Ark of the Covenant, and Abinadab the older brother of David.
H0041H.emploi: Abinadab, son of Saul, is mentioned only in the account of the battle of Gilboa and his royal genealogy. He appears only four times: twice in 1 Samuel 31:2 and 1 Chronicles 10:2 (the account of his death in battle), and twice in 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:39 (the genealogical list of Saul's descendants). Unlike his brother Jonathan, Abinadab does not play a significant role in history — he remains a minor figure in Saul's kingdom, known mainly for his royal lineage and his death alongside his father.

sens: Second son of Jesse and older brother of David
H0041I.detail: Abinadab is the second son of Jesse, the father of David. He appears in the account where the prophet Samuel comes to Bethlehem to anoint a new king in place of Saul. When Samuel examines Jesse's sons, Abinadab is presented after his older brother Eliab, but he is not the one chosen by God — it is David, the youngest, who will be anointed (1 Samuel 16:8). Later, at the time when David faces Goliath, Abinadab is among the three oldest sons of Jesse who followed Saul to war, confirming that he was a man of his generation called to military service (1 Samuel 17:13).
H0041I.origine: The name Abinadab means "my father is noble" or "my father is willing," composed of "father" and an adjective expressing nobility or willingness. It is a typical Hebrew name from David's family, reflecting familial piety.
H0041I.emploi: Abinadab appears three times in the Bible, always as the son of Jesse and brother of David. First in 1 Samuel 16:8, during the selection of David as king by Samuel in Bethlehem, where he is rejected as anointed. Then in 1 Samuel 17:13, where he is mentioned among the three eldest who accompany Saul to war against the Philistines at the time David faces Goliath. Finally, in 1 Chronicles 2:13, in the genealogy of Jesse which lists his sons in order of birth. These three references position Abinadab as a secondary figure during the establishment of David.

sens: father of Barak
man of the tribe of Naphtali
warrior during the time of the Judges
H0042.detail: Abinoam is the father of Barak, the warrior whom the prophetess Deborah calls to fight Sisera and the Canaanite army (Judges 4:6). His Hebrew name literally means "my father is delight" or "my father is joy," expressing a filial trust in God. Although Abinoam himself is never shown in action, his son Barak becomes an important military leader under Deborah's guidance, and it is through his lineage that Abinoam is mentioned four times in the text of Judges (4:6, 4:12, 5:1, 5:12). Deborah's victory song celebrates Barak as "son of Abinoam" as the one who led Israel to deliverance.
H0042.origine: The name is formed from two Hebrew words: "Abi" (my father) and "Noam" (delight, sweetness, pleasantness). It expresses a personal relationship of trust in God, like many names from ancient Israel that proclaim divine goodness or power.
H0042.emploi: Abinoam appears only in the book of Judges, always as the father of Barak. He lived during the time of the Judges, before the Israelite monarchy. In the four passages where he is named, it is solely to identify Barak: Deborah calls him by specifying that he is the "son of Abinoam" (Judges 4:6), and this title of lineage is maintained in the account of his march to Mount Tabor (Judges 4:12), then in the victory song (Judges 5:1 and 5:12). His role is limited to that of the father of a hero of faith.

sens: Member of the tribe of Levi, descendant of Korah
H0043.detail: Ebiasaph is a Levite from the Old Testament whose name means "my father has gathered." He appears in the genealogies of the tribe of Levi as the son (or descendant) of Korah and ancestor of a Levitical branch that served as temple guardians. In 1 Chronicles 6:23, he is listed in the genealogical succession: "Elkanah, his son; Ebiasaph, his son; Assir, his son." The descendants of Ebiasaph, called Korahites, kept the thresholds of the tent of the Lord, as reported in 1 Chronicles 9:19, where it is said that "their fathers had kept the entrance of the camp of the Lord." His name also appears in other forms in the genealogies: he is mentioned as Abiasaph in Exodus 6:24 and as Asaph in 1 Chronicles 26:1.
H0043.origine: The name Ebiasaph (אברסף in Hebrew) literally means "my father has gathered," composed of Abi ("my father") and Asaph ("has gathered"). This form of the name reflects an acknowledgment of divine providence through the genealogy of this family. He himself, son of Korah, is the ancestor of an important lineage of Levites who maintained central religious responsibilities in the service of Israel's sanctuary.
H0043.emploi: Ebiasaph appears three times in the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles, always as a link in a chain of descendants. He is identified as the son of Elkanah and father (or ancestor) of Assir, and he also appears in another genealogy in 1 Chronicles 6:37. The richest context is found in 1 Chronicles 9:19, where his Levitical descendants, the Korahites, are presented as the guardians of the thresholds of the temple. This mention shows that his lineage played an important liturgical role: his ancestors had kept the entrance of the camp of the Lord in the wilderness, and this function was perpetuated by his descendants at the time of the temple.

sens: Warrior of David, military leader of Israel during the united monarchy
H0044G.detail: Abiézer is a military officer of King David, originally from Anathoth (a city of Benjamin). He appears in the lists of the "Thirty," the elite warriors of King David. He also commanded a division of twenty-four thousand men in the army of Israel, responsible for the defense of the country during the ninth month of each year. His name means "my father is help," reflecting a trust in divine assistance.
H0044G.origine: The name Abiézer means "my father is help" (abi = my father, ézer = help). It is a theophoric name, composed of a familial relationship and an invocation for divine help — a common structure in ancient Hebrew names. This type of name reveals the faith of the parents at the time of the child's birth.
H0044G.emploi: Abiézer appears three times in the Scriptures, all in the books of Samuel and Chronicles, which list David's warriors. He is mentioned in 2 Samuel 23:27 and 1 Chronicles 11:28 among the "Thirty" elite warriors of King David, and in 1 Chronicles 27:12 where he is named commander of the royal division for the ninth month, overseeing twenty-four thousand soldiers. He is each time identified as coming from Anathoth.
H0044G.portee: Abiézer embodies faithful service and dedication to God and his king. His name, which means "my father is help," reminds us that military victory relies on trust in divine assistance, not merely on the strength of arms. His integration into David's elite warrior group shows how God elevates faithful men to positions of responsibility and influence.

sens: Man of the tribe of Manasseh during the divided monarchy
H0044H.detail: Abiézer is a man of the tribe of Manasseh mentioned only once in the Old Testament. He is presented as the son or grandson of Gilead and the brother of Ishhod and Machlah (1 Chronicles 7:18). His name means "my father is help" or "my father helps," expressing the trust that the father places in God as a source of help and protection.
H0044H.origine: The name Abiézer is composed of two Hebrew elements: "abi" meaning "my father" and "ézer" meaning "help" or "assistance." This composition reflects a common theology in the Old Testament where names express a relationship to God or a prayer. The name reveals the father's faith in God as protector and provider.
H0044H.emploi: Abiézer is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:18, in a genealogical list of the tribe of Manasseh. He is named there among the children or grandchildren of Gilead, alongside his brothers Ishhod and Machlah. These genealogies in the book of Chronicles serve to establish the lineage of the tribes of Israel and the territorial inheritance of each. Although few details are given about his personal life, his mention in this record ensures his place in the history of Israel.

sens: Clan of the tribe of Manasseh
Warrior of David
H0044I.detail: 1. Abiézer is first the name of a clan that belongs to the tribe of Manasseh. This clan descends from Gilead and receives a portion of the territory of Canaan at the time of the land distribution (Joshua 17:2). 2. By extension, the name also designates a warrior who fought alongside Gideon; Abiézer is called to march after Gideon when he prepares to fight the Midianites (Judges 6:34). The name can also refer to the entire territory or region occupied by this clan, as seen in Judges 8:2 where the "vintage of Abiézer" refers to the resources or population of that region.
H0044I.origine: The name Abiézer literally means "my father is help" or "my father is assistance," formed from two elements: "abi" which means "my father" and "ézer" which means "help" or "assistance." It is a theophoric name, expressing trust in the divine help of the Father. Abiézer also appears in the form Jezer (mentioned in Numbers 26:30), a variant of the same name.
H0044I.emploi: Abiézer appears three times in the Bible as a proper name. It first designates a family or clan of Manasseh, whose members receive a portion of land in Canaan (Joshua 17:2). Then, the name is associated with Gideon in the context of the wars against the Midianites: Abiézer is the clan or region from which Gideon's army comes (Judges 6:34 and 8:2). These two passages show the military and territorial importance of this clan during the time of the Judges.

sens: Warrior in King David's army
H0045.detail: Abi-Albon is a warrior mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of David's "mighty men" (2 Samuel 23:31). He hails from Araba and is part of the king's elite military force.
H0045.origine: The name means "El (God) is my father" in Hebrew. There is also a variant of the name: Abiel, which carries the same meaning. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common in Israel to express trust in divine protection.
H0045.emploi: Abi-Albon appears only once in Scripture, in 2 Samuel 23:31, where he is included in the list of the thirty elite warriors who served under David. This list enumerates the king's most faithful and formidable heroes, each recognized for their valor in battle. His inclusion in this prestigious list shows that he was a valued and experienced fighter, although Scripture does not report any details of his particular exploits.

sens: One who possesses exceptional strength and vigor
One who dominates by strength, authority
God in His omnipotence
Poetic and solemn title of God related to His protective strength
H0046.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes physical strength, vigor — a manifest and effective power. In Genesis 49:24, it is by the "hands of the Mighty One of Jacob" that Joseph's hands were strengthened, an image of a force that acts concretely.
2. What is powerful dominates and triumphs: that is why Isaiah 1:24 applies it to the Lord who will take satisfaction from His adversaries — power implies authority and victory.
3. The word serves as a divine name: "the Mighty One of Jacob" in Psalms 132:2 and Psalms 132:5 designates God Himself by His invincible strength, without any other qualifier.
4. It is a poetic and archaic title, solemn, that emphasizes God as protector and defender: "your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob" in Isaiah 49:26, where power saves and liberates.
H0046.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root expressing strength and vigor. The form corresponds to that of an adjective or noun designating one who has strength. It appears only in religious or poetic contexts, applied exclusively to God: it is a term of veneration, a relic of the ancient liturgical language of Israel.
H0046.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the singular, never to describe a human or creature. At least four times (Psalms 132, Isaiah 49:26 and 60:16), it appears in apposition: "the Mighty One of Jacob," a title that is passed down through generations, associated with the idea of salvation and redemption. Only once (Isaiah 1:24), it is the "Mighty One of Israel" who speaks and acts as judge. The context is always that of divine protection, salvation, the strength that triumphs over evil and defends the weak people.
H0046.portee: This word teaches that God's power is not abstract: it acts, it protects, it saves. It strengthens the weak and crushes the enemy. Calling God "the Mighty One" is not admiring brute force, but recognizing in Him the only reliable support, the one who will never fail in the face of adversity.

sens: Male and powerful animal of the cattle herd
Courageous and strong warrior
Violent and formidable enemy
Powerful prince or leader
Stubborn and brute force
H0047G.detail: 1. The bull is primarily the animal that everyone recognizes: a male ox, vigorous and impressive. The Bible uses it as an image of physical strength. In the Psalms, David describes his enemies as "bulls of Bashan" surrounding him (Psalms 22:13): it is the image of imposing, massive, threatening creatures. 2. The word also designates a warrior, a courageous hero in battle. When the king of Assyria boasts of having "overthrown those who sat on thrones," Scripture calls him a "hero" (Isaiah 10:13): it is the warrior power of a man capable of dominating other powers. 3. The word evokes threat, the enemy charging with rage. The "bulls" of Psalms 68:31 represent a pack of violent adversaries: the image is that of wild, uncontrollable beasts determined to fight. 4. It also describes princes and heads of state, who embody imposing political and military power: one thinks of national powers embodied in their leaders. 5. Finally, the word conveys a kind of stubbornness, brutal will: like a bull charging without listening, without turning aside.
H0047G.origine: The Hebrew word אַבִּיר (abir) comes from a root expressing strength and vigor. It belongs to the family of words that describe physical or moral power. The starting image is clearly that of the bull in its most impressive manifestations: its musculature, its ability to charge, its authority in the herd. This explains why the same word extends to anything that possesses similar strength: warriors, princes, even relentless enemies.
H0047G.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Old Testament. Four times, the Segond translates it as "bull": in the Psalms and in Isaiah, always to evoke real cattle or as a figure of formidable enemies. Once, it is rendered as "hero" (Isaiah 10:13). These uses show that the word oscillates between two worlds: the real (the animal of sacrifice or pasture) and the figurative (the warrior strength, the implacable enemy). In the supplication passages (Psalms 22 and 68), the psalmist uses it to portray his adversaries as fierce and unstoppable beasts. In Isaiah 34:7, it is the day of divine judgment: all the "bulls" fall under God's blows.
H0047G.portee: This word reminds the believer that physical strength, even the most impressive, remains subject to God. The bull, emblem of brute power, falls like any creature when God pronounces His judgment. For the Christian pressed by enemies or oppressed by powers that seem invincible, the biblical text that speaks of the "bulls" shows that these seemingly insurmountable forces do not escape the hand of the Lord. It is an invitation not to fear the violence of this world.

sens: Robust and impetuous horse, with vigorous movements
Characteristic sound of the horse, its neighing
Figuratively: power, vigor, irresistible force
Impulsive, impetuous, untamable character
H0047H.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a war or draft horse, notable for its muscular strength and fiery temperament. In Jeremiah 50:11, the fiery horses leap like a calf in the grass, evoking their overflowing energy and imposing gait.
2. It can also signify the powerful noise made by such a horse: its characteristic neighing. Jeremiah 8:16 and 47:3 describe this sound that resonates and shakes the ground — the neighing here is the audible expression of the horse's strength.
3. By extension, the word applies to any form of power or vigor: that of warriors, angels, even enemies or princes. In Judges 5:22, the hooves of the horses resound, an image of the hurried flight but also of military power in action.
4. The word can also evoke stubbornness, untamability — the stubborn strength of a will that refuses to yield, whether in a creature or a nation.
H0047H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes strength, solidity, and impetuosity. Its primary image is that of the horse, the most powerful and fiery animal known to the ancient Israelites. The root relates to the idea of something robust, imposing, that commands attention through its vigor. In biblical texts, this word applies to both animal creatures and human or spiritual beings that possess this same quality of irrepressible strength.
H0047H.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the books of Judges and Jeremiah, in contexts of war and military power. In Judges 5:22, it describes the hurried flight of Sisera's warriors, whose horses make the ground resound. In Jeremiah (8:16, 47:3, 50:11), it designates the horses of Nebuchadnezzar or Babylon that invade the land: their neighing and the sound of their hooves symbolize the irresistibility of enemy power. The word thus gains a prophetic dimension: the strength of the fiery horse becomes the image of the judgment strength that God allows to be exercised upon His people.
H0047H.portee: This word reminds the believer that true power is not what man sees and fears — the fiery horses of Babylon, the armies that seem invincible. The Bible invites us to place our trust elsewhere: in God alone, whose power infinitely surpasses that of creatures, no matter how imposing they may be. The neighing of the fiery horse also speaks to us of God's judgment, which may seem terrible but is exercised according to divine justice.

sens: One who possesses great physical or moral strength
Who is strong, capable, formidable in action
Who manifests an inflexible, obstinate will
Who has authority, power, dignity
H0047I.detail:
1. The word first describes remarkable physical strength: that of a warrior, a military leader, or an athlete capable of great exploits. In 1 Samuel 21:7, Doeg is called the "chief" of the shepherds, a robust and influential man in the service of the king.
2. It then characterizes moral and political authority — that of princes, warriors, heroes who inspire respect or fear. The "heroes" of Psalm 76:6 are mighty ones who, despite their strength, have been defeated and lie defenseless.
3. The word can also mean "stubborn" or "hardened," a strength of character turned towards evil when it refuses to listen. Isaiah 46:12 speaks of the "hardened" of heart, closed to the word of God — a power turned against God.
4. By extension, the word even applies to animal sacrifices: a powerful, well-formed animal, and thus worthy to be offered. It represents the fullness of strength in all its aspects.
H0047I.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the solidity, the strength of one who stands firm and does not bend. It is related to the notion of physical power and moral firmness. The same root produces other words speaking of strength, power, or resistance. The Hebrew word expresses a concrete reality: the robust body, the unwavering will, the authority that does not doubt.
H0047I.emploi: The word appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poetry (Psalms, Jeremiah) and in wisdom discourse (Job). It describes men of war, princes, enemy warriors: those who embody earthly strength. However, the Bible often uses it to show the impotence of this strength in the face of God — Job 34:20 asserts that the mighty disappears in an instant without anyone touching him. Isaiah 46:12 shifts the meaning towards the hardening of the heart, a moral power deployed against God. Jeremiah 46:15 reports the fall of Pharaoh's valiant men, overwhelmed by the Lord.
H0047I.portee: This word invites the Christian reader not to confuse earthly power with true spiritual strength. The mighty men of the world — warriors, princes, businessmen — may seem invincible and hardened in their pride. Yet, the Bible asserts that only God possesses true power. The hardening of the heart, this perverted form of strength, is a warning: power only makes sense when submitted to God.

sens: One who has great strength, great power
A celestial or divine being
A leader, a prince, a person of authority
An insurmountable or formidable force
That which is robust, solid, unshakeable
H0047J.detail:
1. The word first designates one who possesses great physical or moral strength: a valiant warrior, a man of power. It is the image of the strong, of one who dominates by his vigor.
2. It also applies to angels or celestial beings, powerful creatures of the divine realm. In Psalms 78:25, "the bread of the mighty" refers to the bread of angels, that is, the manna that God sent from heaven: these "mighty ones" are the messengers and servants of God.
3. It qualifies princes and leaders, those who exercise authority and command over a people or an army.
4. It can describe a formidable enemy, an opposing force that cannot be easily defeated.
5. It also expresses the idea of obstinacy or rigidity: something solid, that does not bend, that resists.
H0047J.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to be strong" or "to have strength." It belongs to the family of words that express power, vigor, and authority in Hebrew. The starting image is that of muscular strength, of bodily robustness, which then extends to moral, political, and spiritual power.
H0047J.emploi: This word appears rarely in the Hebrew Bible. In the provided usage (Psalms 78:25), it designates the angels themselves, or more precisely the powerful beings of heaven. The context of Psalm 78 is that of Israel's history in Egypt and in the desert: by speaking of the bread of the "mighty" or the bread of angels, the psalmist magnifies the manna as a food of superhuman essence, sent by the very power of God. The word emphasizes both the greatness of the beings who brought it and the extraordinary generosity of God towards His people.
H0047J.portee: This word reminds us that behind the miracles and gifts of God stand celestial powers, and that divine providence infinitely surpasses our human strengths. To see God as "mighty" and His help as coming from the mighty of heaven is to recognize His majesty and to trust in His strength for our own battles.

sens: Son of Eliab from the tribe of Reuben during the time of the Exodus
Leader of a revolt against Moses and Aaron alongside Dathan and Korah
Rebellion against the order established by God
H0048G.detail:
1. Abiram is a Reubenite, son of Eliab, living during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness journey. He is known from the account in Numbers 16, where he first appears alongside Korah and Dathan.
2. Abiram revolts against Moses and Aaron, refusing to go up to the assembly that Moses summoned (Numbers 16:12) and standing at the entrance of his tent with his family to contest the established authority (Numbers 16:27).
3. His rebellion represents a serious act of disobedience against God and His representatives: he and his household are swallowed up by the earth that opens beneath them in divine judgment, as recalled in Psalm 106:17.
H0048G.origine: The name Abiram literally means "my father is exalted" or "the Exalted (i.e., God) is my father." It is composed of two Hebrew roots: "abi" (father) and "ram" (exalted, lifted up). This name suggested a privileged relationship with God, making Abiram's rebellion all the more ironic: one who bears a name evoking divine fatherhood chooses to rebel against the God he claimed to honor.
H0048G.emploi: Abiram is mentioned eight times in the provided usages, primarily in the account of his revolt in Numbers 16. He acts as an accomplice of Dathan during the uprising against Moses and Aaron: first cited alongside Korah and Dathan as a leader of the revolt (Numbers 16:1), he refuses Moses' authority (Numbers 16:12) and ultimately perishes with his entire household when the earth opens beneath him. Deuteronomy 11:6 and Psalm 106:17 recall this event as an example of divine judgment on rebellion.
H0048G.portee: The story of Abiram teaches the seriousness of rebellion against the order established by God. Although his name promises a privileged relationship with the Heavenly Father, his rebellion leads to total destruction. For the Christian, this account invites reflection on whether their own actions reflect respect for the authority that God has established and warns of the consequences of refusing to submit to God's will as expressed by His servants.

sens: eldest son of Hiel of Bethel
H0048H.detail: Abiram is the eldest son of Hiel, a man from Bethel who undertook to rebuild the city of Jericho. According to 1 Kings 16:34, Hiel would have founded Jericho "at the cost of Abiram," meaning that the young man died during this reconstruction, thus fulfilling a curse pronounced long ago by Joshua (see Joshua 6:26).
H0048H.origine: The name Abiram means "my father is exalted" or "the Exalted Father." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: "ab" (father) and "ram" (exalted, lifted up). It is a theophoric name, expressing a relationship between the father and the deity.
H0048H.emploi: Abiram appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 16:34. He is mentioned as the eldest son of Hiel the Bethelite, who rebuilt Jericho during the divided monarchy (reign of Ahab). His death during the construction illustrates the fulfillment of the divine judgment pronounced by Joshua against anyone who would rebuild the walls of Jericho.
H0048H.portee: The fate of Abiram serves as a reminder that God's words do not go unfulfilled: the judgment of the Lord, pronounced generations earlier, always comes to pass. His story warns of the consequences of disobeying divine decrees and the respect that the fulfillment of God's will deserves.

sens: Young woman from Shunem who cared for King David in his old age
Woman whom Prince Adonijah requested in marriage after David's death
H0049.detail:
1. Abischag was a beautiful young girl from the city of Shunem, whom King David's servants sought to care for the ailing old king: she warmed him with her presence and attended to his daily needs (1 Kings 1:3-4).
2. After David's death, Adonijah, the king's son and claimant to the throne, requested King Solomon to give him Abischag in marriage, which provoked Solomon's anger, as he saw it as an attempt to maintain his rights to the kingship as heir (1 Kings 2:17-22).
H0049.origine: The name Abischag literally means "my father is a wanderer" or "my father wanders." It is a Hebrew name composed of "abi" (father) and "shag" (to wander, to roam). Few details are given about her origins before entering the service of King David.
H0049.emploi: Abischag appears five times in the first book of Kings, all in chapters 1 and 2. She is first presented as the young woman chosen to care for David in his old age (1 Kings 1:3-4, 15). Then she becomes a political pawn: after the king's death, Adonijah claims her hand in marriage (1 Kings 2:17), and Solomon refuses this request, recognizing that it conceals a claim to the throne (1 Kings 2:21-22). Abischag remains a silent figure, an object of desire but never an actor in the narrative.
H0049.portee: The story of Abischag illustrates how a woman can become a political pawn without having a voice in the matter. It reminds the reader that behind the power struggles at the royal court are real people, reduced to political instruments. Her role as caregiver to old David humanizes the great king in his weakness.

sens: Member of the tribe of Levi, grandson of Aaron
Ancestor of the priestly lineage of Ezra
H0050G.detail: Abischua is a man from the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness. He is the son of Phinehas and the grandson of Aaron, the first high priest of Israel (1 Chronicles 6:4). He is also a distant ancestor of the priest Ezra: Ezra 7:5 mentions him in his direct lineage, showing that this priestly lineage has been perpetuated through generations until the return from exile in Babylon.
H0050G.origine: The name Abischua means "my father is help" or "my father is wealth," composed of "father" and a term expressing protection or abundance. This theophoric name — which includes an affirmation about God the Father — reflects the piety of Levitical families.
H0050G.emploi: Abischua appears four times in the Bible, all in genealogies. Twice in 1 Chronicles 6 (verses 4 and 5), where he is situated between Phinehas and Bukki in the priestly lineage. He also appears in 1 Chronicles 6:50, listing the sons of Aaron, and finally in Ezra 7:5, where he figures in the official genealogy of the priest Ezra upon the return from exile. These occurrences underscore the importance of tracing legitimate priestly ancestry.

sens: Man from the tribe of Benjamin during the time of Egypt and the wilderness
H0050H.detail: Abischua is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Bela and the brother of several other men: Ard, Naaman, Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, Iri, Addar, Gera, Abihud, and Ahoach (1 Chronicles 8:4).
H0050H.origine: The name Abischua means "my Father is deliverance" or "my Father is wealth." It carries the idea of protection or abundance that comes from God, the Father. Although this character is not well known, his name expresses trust in divine goodness.
H0050H.emploi: Abischua appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:4, in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. He is presented as the son of Bela, a member of an important family in this tribe. This genealogical passage reminds us that every name in Scripture, even the least known, has significance in the history of God's people.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
H0051.detail: Abischur is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, living at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms. He appears in the genealogies of Judah as the son of Shammai and brother of Nadab (1 Chronicles 2:28).
H0051.origine: The name Abischur means "my father is a wall." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: "abi" (my father) and "shur" (wall). It is a typical theophoric name from the ancient Near East, evoking the protection and solidity that a father—or symbolically God as a protective father—represents.
H0051.emploi: Abischur is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 2, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Judah. He was the son of Shammai, married to Abichail, and had two sons: Achban and Molid (1 Chronicles 2:28-29). These mentions place Abischur in the genealogical chain of Judah, without reporting any particular event from his life.

sens: Israelite warrior, son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab and Asahel
Military chief of David and commander of troops
Nephew of King David
H0052.detail:
1. Abischaï is a warrior and military chief of Israel under the reign of David, belonging to the famous family of the three sons of Zeruiah: himself, Joab, and Asahel. He first appears in 1 Samuel 26:6, where he accompanies David on the nighttime expedition to Saul's camp and offers to strike him.

2. As a military commander, Abischaï leads his own troops during David's campaigns, notably against the Ammonites and the Syrians (2 Samuel 10:14), where he pursues the fleeing enemy. According to 1 Chronicles 11:20, he is the chief of the three (his brothers) and kills three hundred men by himself, thus gaining great renown.

3. Abischaï is also the nephew of King David through his mother Zeruiah, David's sister. This familial proximity places him in the immediate entourage of the king and gives him significant responsibilities in the military and political affairs of the kingdom.
H0052.origine: The name means "my father is Jesse" or "my father is a gift." Jesse was the father of King David, which explains why Abischaï carries in his name the genealogical link with this revered ancestor. He is the grandson of Jesse and the son of Zeruiah, David's sister.
H0052.emploi: Abischaï appears in twenty-four verses, primarily in the books of Samuel and Chronicles, in accounts related to the wars and challenges of David's reign. He intervenes early on, in 1 Samuel 26, when David chooses him to accompany him to the sleeping Saul. He plays a key role in the campaigns against the Ammonites and the Syrians (2 Samuel 10), and he is called to participate in the pursuit of the rebels like Sheba son of Bichri (2 Samuel 20:10). Abischaï is also present during the rebellion of Absalom (2 Samuel 18:5), where David entrusts his generals, including Abischaï, with the task of dealing gently with the young rebel. His military exploits and loyalty to David make him one of the king's most reliable officers.
H0052.portee: Abischaï illustrates fidelity and devotion to the Lord's anointed king. His readiness to accompany David and obey his orders, even difficult ones, shows how a servant of the Lord can remain loyal and useful, despite challenges and dangers. His warrior strength in service to David also symbolizes how God strengthens his servants to fulfill his will in the history of his people.

sens: third son of King David
the one who killed his brother Amnon to avenge his sister's honor
the one who rebelled against his father David to take the throne
figure of rebellion and pride that leads to destruction
H0053.detail:
1. Absalom is the third son of King David and Maacah, daughter of a neighboring king (2 Samuel 3:3). He is the brother of several royal princes, including the firstborn Amnon.
2. After his brother Amnon commits an outrage against their sister Tamar, Absalom has him killed during a feast (2 Samuel 13). This act of vengeance is meant to restore the family's honor, but it forces Absalom to flee to the king of Geshur, from whom his mother was descended (2 Samuel 13:37).
3. Upon returning to Jerusalem, Absalom becomes popular: he rises early at the city gate to welcome those in need of justice, wins their favor, and gains their trust (2 Samuel 15:2-4). He then secretly plots a rebellion: he announces a pilgrimage to Hebron but secretly proclaims his kingship (2 Samuel 15:7-10).
4. The figure of Absalom embodies pride, vengeance, and rebellion against paternal authority. Although handsome and charming, he is consumed by resentment, and his quest for power leads him to challenge his father David himself. He ultimately dies in battle, plunging David into deep mourning (2 Samuel 18:33).
H0053.origine: The name Absalom means "my father is peace" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: "ab" (father) and "shalom" (peace). This name reflects a striking contrast with the character's fate: while his name evokes peace, Absalom will be the author of divisions, murders, and civil war. This contrast between the meaning of the name and the character's actions is one of the tragic ironies of his story.
H0053.emploi: Absalom appears 92 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the book of 2 Samuel, which details his life. His story spans from 2 Samuel 3 (his birth) to 2 Samuel 19 (the aftermath of his death). The accounts show him first as a son seeking vengeance (2 Samuel 13), then as a political and charming prince (2 Samuel 15:1-6), and finally as a rebel in open war against his father (2 Samuel 15-18). The Segond refers to him once as "Abisalom" (in 1 Kings 15:2), reflecting a variant of the name. His story illustrates how ambition and resentment can corrupt even one who is of royal descent.
H0053.portee: The story of Absalom warns the reader of the consequences of pride and rebellion. It shows how charm and manipulation can seduce a crowd, and how vengeance, even seemingly just, opens the door to further misfortunes. The figure of Absalom also reminds us of the pain of the betrayed father: David loves his son despite his crimes and mourns his death bitterly, revealing divine mercy even toward one who rebels. For the Christian, it is a lesson on the pitfalls of ambition and the importance of respecting established authority.

sens: priest of Israel during the united monarchy
son of the priest Ahimelech
companion of King David
priest who consults God through the ephod
H0054.detail:
1. Abiathar is a priest of Israel who lived during the time of David and Solomon. His name means "my father is great" in Hebrew. He is the son of Ahimelech, a priest from the family of Eli.
2. When King Saul massacres the priests of Nob, Abiathar is the only survivor: "One son of Ahimelech, son of Ahitub, escaped. His name was Abiathar" (1 Samuel 22:20). He immediately flees to David, who becomes his king and protector.
3. During David's reign, Abiathar serves as a priest and consults God for the king. He wears the ephod, a priestly garment that allows one to know the divine will: "He said to the priest Abiathar, son of Ahimelech: Bring me the ephod!" (1 Samuel 30:7).
4. Along with Zadok, another priest, Abiathar accompanies David in his battles and escapes. He even follows David when he must flee Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15:29).
5. At the end of David's reign, Abiathar supports Adonijah in his attempt to become king instead of Solomon. When Solomon takes power, he deposes him: "So Solomon removed Abiathar from being priest of the Lord" (1 Kings 2:27).
6. Abiathar represents a priest loyal to the king and his mission, but whose loyalty to a bad heir leads to his downfall.
H0054.origine: The name Abiathar (אֶבְיָתָר) is composed of two Hebrew elements: "abi" (אָבִי) meaning "my father" and "yatar" (יתר) meaning "excellence" or "greatness." Literally, the name means "my father is great" or "the excellence of my father." This etymology reflects the importance of the priestly function in the family of Ahimelech. The name is borne only by this priest in the Hebrew Bible.
H0054.emploi: Abiathar appears 29 times in the translations of Segond, mainly in the books of Samuel and Kings. He is first introduced as the son of Ahimelech who escaped the massacre at Nob (1 Samuel 22:20-22). For years, he is David's priest and helps him consult God (1 Samuel 23:6, 30:7). He regularly appears alongside David: he accompanies him in exile, stays with him during Absalom's revolt, and is mentioned among his advisors (2 Samuel 8:17, 15:24-29, 20:25). However, at David's death, Abiathar chooses the wrong candidate for the throne: he supports Adonijah against Solomon (1 Kings 1:7, 1:25). This mistake costs him dearly: Solomon removes him from his priestly duties (1 Kings 2:27), thus fulfilling an ancient word against the house of Eli (1 Samuel 2:31-33). Abiathar's trajectory shows how even a pious man can make grave mistakes in political choices.
H0054.portee: Abiathar teaches that faithfulness to the Lord is not measured solely by loyalty to a person or cause, even if just at the outset. His support for Adonijah, against God's choice for Solomon, shows that pious men can misdiscern God's will. His deposition reminds us that God governs history and that human choices have consequences. For the reader, Abiathar invites us to seek divine wisdom rather than blindly follow men, even venerable ones.

sens: To rise up, to unfold upwards
To unfold, to gradually extend into the air
H0055.detail:
1. The word describes the movement of something that rises, unfolding towards the sky. In Isaiah 9:17, it is the smoke that "rises" in columns above the burning forest: the image is one of gradual and visible ascent.
2. More broadly, it conveys the idea of something that unfolds, develops upwards, like a scroll being unrolled or a cloud rising. The Hebrew verb evokes this upward unfolding movement.
H0055.origine: The Hebrew verb אָבַךְ (avakh) comes from a root that expresses the idea of rolling, unfolding. In the Hithpael (a reflexive form of Hebrew), it literally means "to roll oneself, to unfold": hence the image of smoke that unfolds and spirals up towards the sky, like something that gradually unfolds.
H0055.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 9:17. It describes the smoke that rises from the forest consumed by wickedness and the fire of divine judgment. It is a poetic term chosen to evoke the graceful and inevitable movement of smoke rising, perhaps symbolizing the visible and ongoing ascent of the destruction of evil.
H0055.portee: This word invites reflection on the reality of divine judgment: wickedness has visible and inevitable consequences, manifest like smoke rising before everyone's eyes. It is a call to repentance, for what is hidden or denied will be revealed as clearly as smoke rises into the sky.

sens: To express one's pain and sorrow through gestures and words, generally after a death or great misfortune.
To mourn, that is, to wear sackcloth, fast, and withdraw to honor the dead.
To show sadness or dismay in the face of a loss, destruction, or serious event.
To lament, to weep long and openly over someone or something lost.
To express the grief of a community or people in the face of a collective disaster.
To personify desolation or sadness — the land, the walls, the gates themselves "mourn."
H0056.detail:
1. To mourn means first to show one's grief visibly and ritually, especially after the death of a close person. David "mourned for a long time for his son" (Genesis 37:34): Jacob tore his clothes and put on sackcloth, classic gestures of mourning in the ancient Near East.
2. It also involves performing mourning rites: fasting, weeping, withdrawing from the world for a time. Nehemiah "wept and was in mourning for several days" (Nehemiah 1:4), thus expressing his deep sorrow over the ruin of Jerusalem.
3. The word also denotes a reaction of sadness or dismay in the face of any serious loss, not just death. The inhabitants of Samaria "will mourn for the idol" that disappears (Hosea 10:5) — it is a lamentation over the loss of what they cherished.
4. Figuratively, things themselves "mourn": the land, the walls of Zion "are plunged into mourning" (Lamentations 2:8), and the gates "become desolation" (Isaiah 3:26). This striking image expresses how a disaster affects even inanimate things, so total is it.
H0056.origine: The Hebrew verb אָבַל comes from a primitive root that first evokes the idea of loss and sorrow. Its basic meaning is "to be afflicted, to mourn." In the Hebrew Scriptures, mourning is a profound social and religious act, accompanied by visible gestures (tearing of clothes, wearing sackcloth, fasting) that manifest inner suffering. The word also has a causative form (Hiphil) meaning "to cause to weep, to bring about mourning."
H0056.emploi: This verb appears 38 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in historical narratives (Samuel, Chronicles), prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, Amos), and Lamentations. David "wept" for his son after the announcement of his death (2 Samuel 13:37). The word is also used to express the collective mourning of a city or nation: the inhabitants "mourn" over the destroyed Jerusalem (Isaiah 66:10). A remarkable poetic figure makes the land itself "mourn" when evil or judgment affects the people (Isaiah 24:4, Jeremiah 4:28, Amos 1:2): mourning becomes a cosmic reaction to sin or misfortune.
H0056.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that sadness in the face of loss is not only natural but also a dignified and even pious act: we must weep with those who weep. It also reveals how the Bible takes human grief seriously — it does not ask us to stifle it, but to express it openly before God. Finally, the image of cosmic mourning shows that sin and judgment affect all of creation, deepening our understanding of salvation: Christ restores not only souls but all of creation.

sens: To mourn, to grieve for a deceased person
To experience sorrow, desolation in the face of misfortune
One who is in mourning or in sorrow
The rites and gestures of mourning
H0057.detail: 1. Afflicted primarily means to be struck by the death of a loved one and to enter into mourning. It is the state of one who weeps for the dead, who mourns according to customs. Mordecai in Esther 6:12 is 'distressed' and covers his head after the misfortunes of the Jews: this is the gesture of mourning. 2. The word also denotes general sorrow in the face of disaster or any misfortune, not just death. In Isaiah 57:18, God comforts those who 'mourn,' meaning those who suffer from various afflictions. 3. Afflicted can also be a noun to designate one who suffers, the bereaved person. Job 29:25 mentions the comforter 'beside the afflicted': one who relieves those who bear grief or pain. 4. The word also encompasses the gestures and rites of mourning: covering oneself with sackcloth, veiling the head, walking slowly. Psalm 35:14 illustrates this: 'I walked about mournfully' as a sign of mourning, 'I bowed down in sorrow.'
H0057.origine: The Hebrew word אָבֵל (a.vel) comes from a root that expresses the idea of bowing down, bending under the weight of grief. It is related to the state of one who bends the body and soul under the blow of a loss. Words from the same family describe pain, suffering, and the gesturing of mourning. In Hebrew, mourning is never silent: it is an attitude that is shown by the whole body.
H0057.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books and the prophets. In Genesis 37:35, Jacob refuses to be comforted in his mourning for Joseph. In the passages from Isaiah (57:18, 61:2-3), the focus shifts from mourning for the dead to the afflicted in general: the prophetic text broadens the term to all who suffer and need comfort. Psalm 35:14 and Lamentations 1:4 describe the rites of mourning: dragging oneself, bowing down, veiling the head. Esther 6:12 shows how Haman returns home 'distressed,' revealing how affliction is read on the face and in the bearing of the body.
H0057.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide the pain of loss: it is normal, it manifests, and it deserves to be borne together. But afflicted also carries a message of hope: all the prophetic passages promise comfort, healing, and joy to those who mourn. It is a call not to hide one's sorrow, and a promise that God sees the pain and transforms it.

sens: Place where the ark stopped in the field of Joshua at Beth-Shemesh
H0059G.detail: 1. It is the name of the rock or large stone on which the ark of the covenant stopped when it was brought back from the land of the Philistines. The word 'abel' literally means 'stone' in Hebrew. In 1 Samuel 6:18, this specific place is mentioned as the witness of the miraculous return of the ark: the Levites offered burnt offerings and sacrifices on this stone, thus marking the end of the ark's journey and its arrival at Beth-Shemesh.
H0059G.origine: The Hebrew word abel comes from a root that designates stone. It is a concrete term that names a remarkable physical object: the large stone that served as a base or support point during the return of the ark. This geographical name has thus preserved the memory of a pivotal event in the history of Israel.
H0059G.emploi: This term appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 6:18, in the account of the return of the ark of the covenant. It designates the exact place and the specific stone where the Levites celebrated the return of the ark with sacrifices. This local proper name marked this moment as a holy place of remembrance for Israel.

sens: Fortified city in northern Israel
Center of wisdom and counsel in ancient Israel
H0059H.detail:
1. Abel is a fortified city located in northern Israel, near Beth-Maaca. It was an established urban center, capable of withstanding sieges and exercising authority in the region (2 Samuel 20:18).
2. The city was famous for its wisdom: people came there seeking counsel and solutions to conflicts, as one might do in other cities renowned for their discernment. Its very name evokes this reputation for prudence and good judgment.
H0059H.origine: The Hebrew name אָבֵל (Abel) literally means 'meadow' or 'pasture' (from the root evoking grass and green space). It is a city in northern Israel that also bears the full name of Abel-Beth-Maaca (אָבֵל בֵּית־מֲעַכָה), which means 'meadow of the house of Maaca.' The name may highlight the fertility or the cultivated nature of the site.
H0059H.emploi: Abel appears only once in the Bible as an abbreviated form of the name: in 2 Samuel 20:18, during the siege of the city by Joab during Absalom's rebellion. A wise woman from the city speaks to Joab and reminds him that the proverb said 'Let them consult Abel!', which shows that Abel was renowned for its wisdom and for the counsel obtained there. This unique mention confirms that the city enjoyed a special reputation for discernment among the cities of Israel.

sens: Sorrow and affliction caused by the death of a person
The set of rites and practices that express mourning
Special clothing worn as a sign of mourning
The period during which one mourns
H0060.detail:
1. Mourning is primarily the intense pain caused by the death of someone. It is a deep feeling of sadness and affliction: when one learns of the death of a loved one, one enters into mourning. Esau, for example, waits for his father's death to kill Jacob, thinking that 'the days of mourning' for his father are approaching (Genesis 27:41).
2. Mourning also refers to the rites and practices that mark this sorrow: weeping, lamentations, gestures of dismay. The children of Israel mourned for Moses for thirty days, which constituted 'the days of weeping and mourning for Moses' (Deuteronomy 34:8).
3. Mourning also encompasses the distinctive clothing worn to show one's grief. A woman who wants to feign mourning must 'dress as a woman in mourning' (2 Samuel 14:2), which implies recognizable clothing.
4. Finally, it is the entire period during which the grieving family observes these practices and wears these marks. During these days of mourning, certain joys are abstained from: the harp becomes 'an instrument of mourning' and can only produce 'plaintive sounds' (Job 30:31).
H0060.origine: The Hebrew word אֵבֶל comes from a root that expresses the idea of weeping and being in mourning. It appears in the context of death and funeral grief. The word belongs to the same family as other Hebrew terms related to sadness and affliction. It is a common word in the Old Testament to describe the process of mourning and all that accompanies it.
H0060.emploi: The word אֵבֶל is used 22 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives (Genesis, 2 Samuel, Esther), in the wisdom books (Job, Ecclesiastes), and in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Micah). It describes both the inner feeling of grief and the external manifestations of mourning: weeping, lamentations, mourning clothes, abstention from certain activities. In Deuteronomy 34:8, it characterizes the official mourning period (thirty days for Moses). Isaiah 60:20 uses it in the future: 'the days of your mourning shall be ended,' evoking divine deliverance from sorrow. The word thus covers both personal emotion and the entire set of social practices that surround it.
H0060.portee: Understanding biblical mourning helps Christians grasp how the Bible recognizes the reality of loss and pain: weeping for the dead is not a lack of faith; it is a human reaction that God Himself honors. But mourning is never final: Isaiah promises that 'the days of your mourning shall be ended,' reminding the believer that death does not have the final word and that God brings comfort. This tension between present pain and future hope is at the heart of Christian redemption.

sens: Marks a strong affirmation, a confirmation
Introduces a restriction or correction
Expresses agreement with what has just been said
H0061.detail:
1. The word strongly and certainly affirms what is announced. When God tells Abraham, "Surely Sarah will bear you a son" (Genesis 17:19), He solemnly confirms His promise. It is the word that seals an important promise or decision.
2. The word can also correct or nuance what precedes, bringing a restriction: "yes, that is true, but..." When Joseph's brothers confess, "Yes, we have been guilty toward our brother" (Genesis 42:21), they acknowledge the fault while explaining it by the context.
3. Finally, it is a simple "yes" that responds to a question or welcomes an affirmation. When the Shunammite woman says, "Yes, I am a widow; my husband is dead" (2 Samuel 14:5), or when Jonathan affirms, "Yes, our lord King David has made Solomon king" (1 Kings 1:43), this word simply validates what has just been stated.
H0061.origine: This Hebrew word belongs to a family of words that express solidity and certainty. It is related to the idea of something established, stable, that holds firm. Its use in oaths and divine confirmations shows its strength: it is the word that makes something truly certain.
H0061.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical accounts of Genesis, the books of Kings and Chronicles, and in the visions of Daniel. It is regularly used in solemn confirmations, such as when God promises something important (Genesis 17:19) or when characters acknowledge a truth (Genesis 42:21). It can also respond to a question or introduce a statement that specifies or corrects what precedes. Depending on the context, it sometimes emphasizes absolute certainty, and other times simple confirmation.
H0061.portee: This word reminds us that the word of God is never spoken lightly: when God says "yes," it is an unshakeable promise. For the reader, it invites recognition of the seriousness of divine commitment and to notice the moments when God seals His will. It is also a word that teaches the importance of a given word: when a man or woman says "yes," it is a serious act that binds.

sens: Fortified city in northern Israel
Place of refuge and siege during civil wars
City conquered by the kings of Aram
H0062.detail:
1. Abel-Beth-Maaca is a fortified city located in northern Israel, near the region of Maachah. Its name means "meadow of the house of Maachah," evoking a fertile place surrounded by defensive walls. It is mentioned as a center of strategic importance.
2. The city became famous as a place of refuge during internal conflicts in the kingdom of Israel. During the rebellion of Sheba against King David, the city is besieged by Joab's army, which builds siege ramps against its walls to bring them down (2 Samuel 20:14-15).
3. Abel-Beth-Maaca also experiences invasions from neighboring kingdoms. It is taken by Ben-Hadad, king of Aram, and later by Tiglath-Pileser III, the king of Assyria, who conquers it during his military campaigns in the Levant.
H0062.origine: The compound name combines Abel ("meadow") and Beth-Maachah ("house of Maachah"). Maachah was a small region or tribe in northern Israel. The name reflects the geography and political organization of the territory: a fertile meadow that belongs to or is associated with the region of Maachah.
H0062.emploi: Abel-Beth-Maaca appears four times in the Old Testament, always in connection with military events. It is first the scene of Sheba's rebellion, a rebel who had "raised the banner against King David" (2 Samuel 20). Joab pursues the rebels there and besieges the city, which triggers a negotiation where the inhabitants hand over Sheba to save their city.
