The city later appears in the annals of Israeli-Aramean conflicts: it is taken by Ben-Hadad (1 Kings 15:20) and ultimately conquered by Tiglath-Pileser III (2 Kings 15:29) during the Assyrian expansion.

sens: Camping site of the Israelites in Moab
Region of the plains, near the Jordan
H0063.detail:
1. Abel-Sittim is a place where the Israelites set up their last camp before crossing the Jordan to enter the Promised Land. The name literally means "meadow of acacias," referring to the shrubs and trees characteristic of this desert region. It is a site mentioned in Numbers 33:49, which lists the stages of the people's journey through the desert.
2. Located in the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, this place was a strategic campsite at the gates of the Promised Land. The Israelites waited there before crossing the river under Joshua's leadership, with the Jordan as the only barrier to cross.
H0063.origine: The name "Abel-Sittim" combines two Hebrew words: "Abel" (אָבֵל), meaning "meadow" or "orchard," and "Shittim" (שִׁטִּים), the plural of "shittah" (שִׁטָּה), the acacia. It is a place named for its characteristic vegetation. The term "Shittim" alone also refers to the place, and various biblical passages refer to this acacia wood used to build the Ark of the Covenant.
H0063.emploi: Abel-Sittim appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 33:49, during the last camping of the Israelites before crossing the Jordan. This passage is part of the recap of the stages of the journey from Egypt. The place geographically and spiritually marks the moment when Israel is about to receive the fulfillment of the promise made to Abraham, yet separated from the Promised Land by the only obstacle of the Jordan.
H0063.portee: Abel-Sittim symbolizes the culmination of the long journey in the desert: the people of God stand at the gates of the promise and must cross one last obstacle. For the Christian reader, this place reminds us that waiting and faith are necessary until the final threshold, and that God never promises without fulfilling.

sens: Region of Ammon located between Aroer and Minnith
H0064.detail: Abel-Keramim is a locality in Ammonite territory, mentioned only once in the Bible during Jephthah's military campaign against the Ammonites. The name literally means "meadow of vineyards" — a place likely fertile, known for its cultivated lands. It marks the southern boundary of the region where Jephthah achieved a decisive victory over the Ammonites (Judges 11:33).
H0064.origine: The name is composed of two Hebrew words: אָבֵל (Abel, "meadow" or "field") and כְּרָמִים (keramim, "vineyards"). It thus designates an agricultural region of Ammon, an ancient kingdom east of the Jordan, known for its lands suitable for grape cultivation.
H0064.emploi: Abel-Keramim appears only once in the provided biblical usages: in Judges 11:33, during Jephthah's victory over the Ammonites. The verse uses this geographical name to trace the extent of the military defeat, between Aroer to the north and Minnith further south, showing that the victory covered a vast region of Ammonite territory.

sens: City of the tribe of Issachar in Israel
Fertile and green region of the Jordan Valley
Birthplace of the prophet Elisha
H0065.detail:
1. Abel-Mehola is a city located in the land of Israel, in the region assigned to the tribe of Issachar. It occupies a strategic position in the Jordan Valley, near the eastern boundary of the Israelite territory. In 1 Kings 4:12, it marks the border of an administrative region: "from Beth-Shean to Abel-Mehola, beyond Jokmeam."
2. The name literally means "meadow of dance" or "dancing meadow," which evokes a pleasant, fertile, and green place, characteristic of the Jordan valleys — a striking contrast to the arid regions of Israel. In Judges 7:22, the fleeing enemies head toward this region: "to the edge of Abel-Mehola."
3. Abel-Mehola is world-renowned as the village of origin of the prophet Elisha, who was born there and received his divine calling. It is here that Elisha was plowing the fields when the prophet Elijah called him to follow and become his successor (1 Kings 19:16).
H0065.origine: The Hebrew name אָבֵל מְחוֹלָה (Abel Mekhola) is composed of two elements: אָבֵל (Abel), meaning "meadow" or "pasture," and מְחוֹלָה (Mekhola), derived from the root חוּל (khoul), meaning "to turn, dance." The name thus paints the image of a meadow where one dances, suggesting a fertile, pleasant, and perhaps lively place, typical of the oases in the Jordan Valley. It is a Semitic geographical name that describes the character of the place.
H0065.emploi: Abel-Mehola appears three times in the Bible, always in the context of the Northern Kingdom of Israel. In Judges 7:22, it appears during Gideon's victory over the Midianites, marking a geographical landmark in the fleeing enemies' route. In 1 Kings 4:12, it serves as an administrative boundary in the territorial organization of Solomon's kingdom. Finally, in 1 Kings 19:16, it is mentioned as the birthplace and home of Elisha before his calling. These three usages place it in the political and religious context of the United Kingdom and its successors, within the context of the Jordan Valley.
H0065.portee: Abel-Mehola reminds us that great prophets of God came from ordinary places and led ordinary lives before their divine calling. Elisha was working at the plow when Elijah met him — he did not expect to change the course of Israel's history. This encourages us to believe that God can call each of us, regardless of our background or station, to serve Him and fulfill His work.

sens: City in northern Israel
Another name for Abel-Beth-Maaca
H0066.detail:
1. Abel-Maïm is a city located in northern Israel during the time of the kings. Its name literally means "meadow of waters" or "pasture of waters," evoking a green and well-watered place. It is mentioned as a military target in the expedition led by the commanders of Ben-Hadad, king of Syria, against the Northern Kingdom (2 Chronicles 16:4).
2. Abel-Maïm is another name for the same locality as Abel-Beth-Maaca, situated in the same region. These two names refer to the same place, known by these two appellations at different times or in different texts.
H0066.origine: The name "Abel-Maïm" combines two Hebrew words: "Abel" (אָבֵל), meaning "meadow" or "pasture," and "Maïm" (מַיִם), meaning "waters." It is a typical place name from the Old Testament, constructed based on the geographical description of the location. The word "Abel" also appears in names like Abel-Shittim (meadow of acacias) or Abel-Keramim. This place likely corresponds to Abel-Beth-Maaca, which is generally located in Upper Galilee or the region of Damascus.
H0066.emploi: Abel-Maïm appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 16:4. It is mentioned in the account of King Asa of Judah's military campaign, who calls upon King Ben-Hadad of Syria for help against the Northern Kingdom. Ben-Hadad sends his generals to strike several Israelite cities, with Abel-Maïm among the targets. This is a historical event from the 9th century BC, illustrating the conflicts between the Northern and Southern kingdoms.

sens: Place of mourning east of the Jordan where the people of Egypt mourned Jacob
H0067.detail: 1. Abel-Mizraïm is a location situated east of the Jordan, on the route between Egypt and Canaan. Its name means "meadow" or "pasture of Egypt," perhaps suggesting a place as fertile as Egypt itself. It is where the funeral procession for Jacob stopped during the return from Egypt to Canaan, and where the Egyptians accompanying the body observed a seven-day mourning period (Genesis 50:11).
H0067.origine: The name Abel-Mizraïm is composed of two words: "Abel" means "meadow" or "pasture" (a fertile valley), and "Mizraïm" refers to Egypt. This place also bears another name, Atad, which means "thorn" or "briar." The contrast between these two names — one evoking fertility, the other aridity — may reflect the two aspects of the site as perceived by those who stopped there.
H0067.emploi: Abel-Mizraïm is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 50:11, during the account of Jacob's death. After Jacob died in Egypt, his sons carried his body to Canaan, accompanied by a large Egyptian entourage. They stopped at Abel-Mizraïm to mourn for seven days, which impressed the local inhabitants of Canaan so much that they named the place "Abel-Mizraïm," meaning "the mourning of Egypt."

sens: Solid rock block, small or large, in its natural state or worked
Raw material for building or manufacturing
Precious stone or gemstone
Object or weapon of destruction
Weight or measure
What symbolizes hardness, strength, and immutability
H0068G.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to stones as they are found or collected: rock blocks of all sizes. In Genesis 28:11, Jacob "took one of the stones of the place" to make a pillow; in Genesis 29:2-3, the shepherds together rolled away the large stone that covered the well.
2. The stone becomes a material for work and construction: it is shaped and fashioned to make walls, altars, and tablets. Leviticus 14:42 speaks of "stones" that are put "in place of the first ones" to repair a house. Exodus 24:12 shows God giving Moses tablets written on stone.
3. Precious stones or "gems" adorn the breastplate of the high priest (Exodus 28:17-21) and symbolize wealth and beauty. Isaiah 60:17 lists the precious materials that God will bring.
4. The stone also serves as a weapon or instrument of punishment: people are stoned with stones (Leviticus 20:2, Deuteronomy 13:10). In 2 Chronicles 26:15, they catapulted "large stones" at the enemies.
5. The stone has weight: it can serve as a commercial weight (1 Samuel 17:49) or a balance weight, establishing a fair measure.
6. Figuratively, the stone evokes immutability, unshakeable solidity: one speaks of a "heart of stone" (hard, insensitive) and in Exodus 15:16, the people "stands still, immobile as stone" before God's miracle — it is stupor, absolute motionlessness.
H0068G.origine: The Hebrew word אֶבֶן comes from an ancient root common to Semitic languages, still in use in Aramaic and Arabic. No other major family of words is related to this root in classical Hebrew: it is an autonomous and fundamental word. The basic notion is simply that of a solid, mineral, immobile mass — a reality so elementary that it does not derive from any older image. It is one of the most concrete and primordial words in the language.
H0068G.emploi: The word is extremely frequent, appearing more than 270 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is found in all historical books (Genesis, Joshua, Kings), in the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), and among the prophets (Isaiah). Its uses cover a wide spectrum: natural stones collected for a pillow or a memorial stone (Genesis 28, Joshua 4); building stones for altars and walls (Deuteronomy 27); precious stones for the priest's adornment (Exodus 28); stones as instruments of judicial stoning (Leviticus, Deuteronomy); stones as projectiles or siege instruments (2 Chronicles 26). The religious context is very present: the tablets of the Law written on stone (Exodus 31:18, Deuteronomy 4:13), the memorials set up by Joshua at the Jordan (Joshua 4:9) to remember God's help. The polysemy is rich but always linked to this concrete core.
H0068G.portee: For the believer, the stone evokes the word of God "written on stone" — immutable, engraved forever, unlike what fades away. It also symbolizes spiritual stability: it is on a rock that Jesus will build His Church (Matthew 16:18). Finally, the stone wall of the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21) expresses the eternity and unshakeable solidity of the kingdom of God.

sens: Stone or object used for weighing, balancing a scale
Mass, weight of a thing
Burden, load one carries
Firmness, solidity, moral stability
Hard heart, insensitivity
H0068H.detail: 1. The primary and most concrete meaning: a stone or any object placed on a scale pan to measure the mass of a commodity. In Israel, stone or metal weights were used for commerce, and the law prohibited having two kinds (a large one and a small one) to defraud (Deuteronomy 25:13). 2. By extension, the weight itself, the heaviness of an object: the hair of Absalom's head weighed two hundred shekels, which is measured in the king's weight (2 Samuel 14:26). 3. In a figurative sense, a burden, a moral or spiritual load one carries. 4. The image of the solid and immobile stone evokes firmness, solidity — a person of weight has authority, stability. 5. Finally, a heart of stone symbolizes insensitivity, hardening towards God: the opposite of sensitivity and obedience.
H0068H.origine: The Hebrew word אֶבֶן comes from an ancient root meaning stone, the hard and stable material. It shares this image with other Semitic languages. The stone, being both common and indestructible, symbolizes in the Bible what is solid, durable, and reliable — but also, when it hardens the heart, what is closed to God. Stone weights were the ordinary instrument of commerce, hence the frequent use of the word to denote commercial weight.
H0068H.emploi: The word אֶבֶן appears 10 times in the provided passages, concentrated in the laws of Deuteronomy and Proverbs. It primarily denotes the practical instrument of commerce: just and false weights (Deuteronomy 25:13, 25:15; Proverbs 11:1, 16:11). It then takes on a more moral sense: having just weights pleases the Lord, false weights are an abomination to Him — the word becomes a symbol of honesty and integrity. There is only one concrete non-commercial occurrence: the weight of Absalom's hair (2 Samuel 14:26), where the word measures a physical reality. The biblical context makes weight the image of what is stable, fair, and trustworthy.
H0068H.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God cares about justice in the small things of commerce and daily life. Just weights are not just a matter of money, but of moral uprightness: "A just weight and balance are the Lord's" (Proverbs 16:11). It is an invitation to integrity in all circumstances, knowing that God scrutinizes the heart as much as our actions.

sens: block or piece of natural rock
hard and compact mineral substance
object serving as a marker or testimony
H0068I.detail:
1. A stone is a block of rock, small or large, found in nature. In 1 Kings 1:9, the stone of Zohéleth is a specific geographical location, a rock or rocky site serving as a marker near En-Rogel, where Adonijah organized a banquet to proclaim himself king.
2. The word also refers to the substance itself, the hard material of which stones are made. It is the raw material of nature.
3. In the Bible, a stone can be a monument or testimony: erected or named, it marks an event or a memorable place, like the stones that Samuel or Joshua erected to remember God's intervention. Here, Zohéleth is probably a well-known natural marker.
H0068I.origine: The Hebrew word אֶבֶן (eben) is very ancient and simply means stone. It is a common name in all Semitic languages. The word appears hundreds of times in the Hebrew Bible, from the Pentateuch to the last books, as stone was omnipresent in daily life and construction. Combined here with Zohéleth ("that slips"), it forms a geographical name: the stone of Zohéleth, a well-identified place in Jerusalem.
H0068I.emploi: The word stone appears very frequently in the Hebrew Bible to denote rocks, mineral blocks, construction materials, or geographical markers. In 1 Kings 1:9, the stone of Zohéleth is a specific site near En-Rogel, a spring southeast of Jerusalem. It is a reference point, known enough to host a large banquet. The name "Zohéleth" likely means "the serpent" or "that which slips," perhaps due to the shape of the rock or a winding stream nearby. In the tense political context of 1 Kings 1, this geographical location marks the stage for a decisive action: the moment when Adonijah attempts to crown himself king against the will of David and Solomon.
H0068I.portee: This passage highlights the importance of places and markers in the biblical collective memory. A simple stone, named and well-known, becomes the stage for royal and political stakes. For the reader, it reminds us that God directs events even in the most ordinary places, and that geography is never neutral in God's plan.

sens: block of natural rock, hard material
material for building structures or walls
object shaped from stone, notably an idol
unyielding force that crushes and transforms
H0069.detail:
1. The stone is primarily a block of rock found in nature — it is the basic raw material. In Ezra 5:8 and 6:4, we speak of "hewn stones," meaning cut and prepared for the construction of the temple.
2. The stone serves as a building material: it forms the walls and foundations of solid and durable buildings. This is why it is used for God's temple in Jerusalem.
3. The stone can be sculpted or shaped into an idol — in Daniel 5:4, the Babylonians praise the "gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone," referring to the statues and idols they worship.
4. In Nebuchadnezzar's dream (Daniel 2:34-35), a mysterious stone breaks off from a mountain and strikes an immense statue, completely shattering it, while the stone itself becomes a great mountain: the image of an unyielding divine power that crushes human kingdoms and fills the whole earth.
H0069.origine: The Hebrew word אֶבֶן comes from a very ancient root, common to Semitic languages, which simply designates stone, solid mineral. It has no particular etymology — it is a primitive word that names a concrete and universal reality. In Ezra and Daniel, which are later texts, this word appears in the same fundamental senses: building material and, in the religious context, the material of idols.
H0069.emploi: The word stone appears 8 times in our references, concentrated in Ezra and Daniel. In Ezra (5:8 and 6:4), it refers to the concrete materials of the temple construction site: "hewn stones" (that is, prepared, squared). In Daniel, the word takes on a symbolic and prophetic significance: in 2:34-35 and 2:45, the "stone" is the central element of a vision that describes the fall of empires before the kingdom of God — it represents the divine power that crushes human kingdoms. In 5:4, it appears among the materials of Babylonian idols. The progression goes from the concrete sense (hewn stone for building) to the theological sense (stone as a symbol of judgment and divine triumph).
H0069.portee: The stone, in the New Testament and according to biblical usage, is associated with solidity, durability, and strength. In Daniel 2, it teaches that the kingdom of God, although starting small and invisible, will crush all human kingdoms and fill the entire earth — a promise of the final triumph of the divine plan over all earthly powers. This symbolism reminds the reader that God is stable, unshakeable, and victorious.

sens: Rotating instrument of the potter for shaping clay
Low seat for midwives during childbirth
H0070.detail: 1. The wheel is the rotating device on which the potter places the clay to shape it: in Jeremiah 18:3, the prophet goes down to see the potter "working at his wheel," an image of the Lord shaping the people as the craftsman shapes the clay. 2. The midwife's seat is a low piece of furniture, often made of two or three stones or a fixed structure, on which women giving birth or the midwives assisting them would sit: in Exodus 1:16, Pharaoh orders the midwives to observe the Hebrew women "on the seats" during childbirth to kill the newborn boys.
H0070.origine: The Hebrew word אֹבֶן (aven or obhen, not to be confused with אֶבֶן eben which means "stone") originally designates any round or rotating object. Its basic image is that of circular movement: the potter's wheel that turns, the round or circular seat of the midwife. These two uses share the circular shape or rotation as a common trait.
H0070.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible in French. In Exodus 1:16, it refers to the low seat used during childbirth: the Hebrew midwives assisted the women sitting on this seat, and Pharaoh wants to use it to identify and eliminate male children. In Jeremiah 18:3, it refers to the potter's wheel, a rotating work instrument; this passage is famous because it becomes a theological image of the Lord shaping Israel as the craftsman shapes the clay. The context changes, but the idea of a useful object capable of transformation remains.
H0070.portee: These two uses illustrate how God controls events: the childbirth seat reminds us that life comes from God alone, despite Pharaoh's plans; the potter's wheel shows that God shapes the history of Israel with sovereign and benevolent authority, like the craftsman with his clay. Meditating on these images helps the believer accept that God shapes our lives according to His will.

sens: Battle site between Israel and the Philistines, north of Jerusalem
Memorial stone raised by the prophet Samuel to mark God's help
H0072.detail:
1. Ebenezer is primarily the name of a place where Israel faced the Philistines. It is where Israel camped to fight, near the place where the Philistines had also set up their camp (1 Samuel 4:1). After this battle, the ark of God was taken by the Philistines and transported from this place (1 Samuel 5:1).
2. The name then designates the stone that Samuel raised as a memorial after God had saved Israel. Samuel took a stone, placed it between Mizpah and Shen, and called it Ebenezer, saying: "Thus far the Lord has helped us" (1 Samuel 7:12). This stone reminded future generations of divine help.
H0072.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "stone (eben) of help (ezer)." It expresses the biblical image of the stone as a lasting monument: a concrete and visible mark of God's intervention. The word "ezer" means help or assistance; it is the same word found when speaking of God's help towards His people. The name itself is a cry of recognition: God has helped Israel, and this stone proclaims it forever.
H0072.emploi: Ebenezer appears three times in the text of Samuel, always in connection with the wars between Israel and the Philistines at the beginning of the monarchy. First, it is the name of the place where the battles took place (1 Samuel 4:1 and 5:1); the battle was lost there, and the ark was captured. Then Samuel raised a memorial stone there (1 Samuel 7:12) to perpetuate the memory of the subsequent victory. The name thus changes in meaning: from a difficult battlefield to a monument of deliverance. It is a reminder that God, despite temporary defeats, remains faithful to His people.
H0072.portee: Ebenezer teaches believers the importance of spiritual memory. This stone raised by Samuel invites each generation to remember God's interventions: "Thus far the Lord has helped us." It is an act of faith that acknowledges that God has guided His people through trials. For the Christian, this speaks to the importance of keeping alive the memory of divine mercies, not out of superstition, but out of gratitude and renewal of trust.

sens: Strip of fabric that wraps around the waist to hold clothing in place
Prestige accessory worn by priests as a sign of their office
Mark of dignity and authority among high officials
H0073.detail:
1. The belt is primarily a strip of fabric placed around the waist to tighten and hold clothing — it can be embroidered or colored, like the fine linen belt embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet (Exodus 39:29).
2. For the priests of the Lord, the belt holds particular significance: it is an integral part of the sacred garment, alongside the tunic, robe, or ephod. It is not only practical but also adorns the priests with dignity and consecration (Exodus 28:4, 28:40).
3. Among high dignitaries, the belt was a sign of rank and authority; the prophet Isaiah refers to it when he announces that a trusted man of the king will receive "the charge like a belt" (Isaiah 22:21), symbolizing the power entrusted to him.
H0073.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of girding, of tightening around. The belt was an essential element of Eastern clothing, serving to hold up long tunics and delineate the sacred part of the body. For the Israelite priests, it was part of a prescription of the Law in which every detail of the priestly garment symbolized a function or spiritual quality.
H0073.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in prescriptions related to worship. Exodus mentions it six times while describing the priestly garments of Aaron and his sons: it is made of fine linen, embroidered or twisted, sometimes colored. Leviticus also mentions it for Aaron and for the sin offering on the Day of Atonement. In Isaiah 22:21, it moves out of the strictly priestly cultic context to become the insignia of political power, showing that the belt represented authority and responsibility in ancient Israel.
H0073.portee: For the Christian, the priest's belt reminds us that serving God requires total consecration and precise order: every detail matters and carries significance. It invites us to see that true dignity does not come from appearance, but from the calling received from God and the respect for the commandments that define it.

sens: Cousin of Saul and commander of his army
Political figure who supported the house of Saul after the king's death
Warrior with a divided heart, ultimately rallies to David
Victim of Joab's vengeance
H0074.detail:
1. Abner is first presented as the military chief of Saul, son of Ner and uncle of the king (1 Samuel 14:50). He holds the title of commander and plays a prominent role alongside the monarch.
2. After Saul's death, Abner becomes the strong man who maintains the dynasty by placing Ishbosheth, son of Saul, on the throne (2 Samuel 2:8-9). He leads the armies of Saul's house against David.
3. Despite his initial loyalty, Abner begins negotiations with David and ultimately switches sides, recognizing that God's will is fulfilled through David (2 Samuel 3:9-19). He becomes a peacemaker and reconciler.
4. As he returns to Hebron after dealing with David, Joab stabs him out of personal vengeance (for the death of his brother Asahel), a betrayal that David publicly condemns (2 Samuel 3:27-28).
H0074.origine: The name Abner means "my father is a lamp" or "my father shines." It comes from the Hebrew word for father (av) and the word for lamp or light (ner). This name was borne during the time of the united monarchy in Israel, in the tribe of Benjamin. Abner's father was Ner, a figure in Saul's inner circle.
H0074.emploi: Abner appears 59 times in the books of Samuel and Kings. He is the key figure in chapters 2 and 3 of 2 Samuel, where his role evolves from the highest to the lowest: first a powerful defender of Saul in war against David, then a negotiator changing alliances, and finally a political victim. After his death, David publicly mourns him and refuses to endorse the murder committed by Joab, showing that men of value do not deserve a disgraceful end (2 Samuel 3:33-37).
H0074.portee: Abner's story teaches that even the powerful of this world are not masters of their destiny, and that human vengeance tarnishes victory. It also shows how God can lead opponents to recognize His will and change sides, but such conversion is never guaranteed a happy ending. For the Christian, Abner remains a complex figure: capable of discerning God's work, yet trapped in conflicts where neither loyalty to the fallen master nor allegiance to the victor can save him from a violent death.

sens: To feed an animal to make it fat and heavy
To make prosperous or well-supplied with food
To indulge in comfort and well-being
H0075.detail:
1. To fatten primarily means to generously feed an animal, particularly an ox or a sheep, to increase its mass of flesh and fat. This is a concrete fact: the well-fed animal becomes "fattened." In 1 Kings 4:23, the text speaks of "fattened oxen" that are among the royal provisions, showing that these fat beasts are a sign of wealth and abundance at the king's table.
2. Figuratively, to fatten can refer to the act of providing someone with food or goods in abundance, making them prosperous. It is to nourish someone generously, ensuring their material well-being.
3. The word also evokes a state of contentment or softness: one who lives in abundance and comfort, surrounded by everything they desire, becomes "fattened" by comfort. In Proverbs 15:17, a "fattened ox" contrasts with "grass for food": one symbolizes ostentatious wealth, the other honest simplicity. The image suggests that material prosperity alone, without love, is worthless.
H0075.origine: The Hebrew verb אָבַס (avas) comes from a root that expresses the idea of nourishing and making grow. Its starting image is that of fattening: giving a lot of food to increase flesh. The word belongs to the vocabulary of livestock and agriculture in ancient Israel, where fat animals represented visible wealth and the prestige of the owner.
H0075.emploi: The verb אָבַס appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. It is found in 1 Kings 4:23 at the heart of the account of King Solomon's daily provisions: it lists the foods destined for his royal table, including fattened oxen, a symbol of luxury and power. The second usage, in Proverbs 15:17, employs it in a moral comparison: faced with the choice between the abundance of meat (a fattened ox) and frugality, the text emphasizes that it is love that constitutes the true wealth of a home. In both cases, the word carries the idea of visible, material wealth that can either be admired or relativized.
H0075.portee: This word reminds us that material wealth — the "fattened oxen" — is not without value in itself: it testifies to God's generosity and the order established within a household or kingdom. But Proverbs warns us: prosperity without love is merely hollow appearance. For the Christian, this invites us to see earthly goods as gifts from God to be enjoyed with gratitude, but never as the foundation of true life — only communion of love with God and others gives value to all abundance.

sens: Small inflamed protuberance that forms on the skin
Manifestation of a skin disease caused by infection or inflammation
H0076.detail:
1. A pustule is a small bump or blister that swells on the skin, filled with infected liquid. It is a painful skin infection: in Exodus 9:9, the ash thrown by Moses "will produce, throughout the land of Egypt, on men and on animals, ulcers formed by an eruption of pustules."
2. The word also refers to the general eruption of these small lesions, which marks the entire body: in Exodus 9:10, the same plague strikes "men and animals" with "ulcers formed by an eruption of pustules." It is a concrete manifestation of God's anger against Egypt.
H0076.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to swell" or "to inflate." It literally describes what rises or buds on the skin: an eruption that elevates. The same family of words is used to talk about anything that swells or becomes tumefied, whether naturally or supernaturally.
H0076.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times during the sixth plague of Egypt (Exodus 9:9-10). It is a very specific term: it is never used for other diseases or in other contexts. The plague of pustules is presented as a direct divine judgment, transforming ash into a cause of disease. This detail emphasizes the supernatural and fearsome nature of God's intervention.
H0076.portee: This word reminds the reader how God demonstrates His power in the face of Pharaoh's refusal, not only through spectacular phenomena (hail, darkness) but also through immediate physical suffering. The plague of pustules directly affects the body, showing that disobedience to God brings concrete, tangible, and unavoidable consequences.

sens: city of the tribe of Issachar
H0077.detail: Abets is a city that belongs to the territory of the tribe of Issachar. It is mentioned in the list of cities that this tribe received during the division of the promised land among the twelve tribes of Israel (Joshua 19:20).
H0077.origine: The name Abets literally means "I will make white" or "I will make muddy," but it primarily designates a geographical location given to Israel. Like many names of ancient cities, its etymology may reveal a characteristic of the terrain or water of the place, but this remains uncertain.
H0077.emploi: Abets appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:20, in the enumeration of the cities assigned to the tribe of Issachar. It is listed among other localities such as Rabbith and Kishion. This brief mention shows that it was a recognized land possession of the Israelite territory, but the Bible provides no further information about its history or significance.

sens: A judge of Israel during the time of the Judges
From Bethlehem
H0078.detail: Ibtsan is one of the minor judges who governed Israel during the period of the Judges, before the establishment of the monarchy. He succeeds Jair and is himself followed by Elon. Bethlehem, his city of origin, is also the place where he was buried after his death.
H0078.origine: The name Ibtsan literally means "their whiteness" or "their brightness," an image related to purity and brilliance. Its exact meaning remains uncertain, but it could refer to tin or something bright white. It is a typical Hebrew name from the context of the Judges.
H0078.emploi: Ibtsan appears twice in the book of Judges, only in chapter 12. He is presented as a judge of Israel after Jair (Judges 12:8), with no details about his exploits or battles. The Bible simply mentions that he had thirty sons and thirty daughters, then that he died and was buried in Bethlehem (Judges 12:10). Unlike other judges like Samson or Gideon, no heroic narrative is associated with him.
H0078.portee: Ibtsan reminds us that God raised leaders to govern His people during a time of instability. His modest, almost discreet story shows that serving God does not always involve spectacular acts, and that even less prominent figures play their role in the divine plan.

sens: To physically confront someone, to embrace and seek to overpower them
To struggle fiercely, refusing to yield
To resist something stronger than oneself
H0079.detail:
1. To struggle denotes a direct physical confrontation, face to face, where two opponents embrace and seek to defeat each other. It is close combat where one attempts to overpower the other by force. Jacob "struggled" with a man all night until dawn (Genesis 32:24): it is not a distant fight, but a struggle in the strict sense, where both protagonists are entwined.
2. To struggle also implies perseverance, tenacity: refusing to give up despite exhaustion. Jacob continued to struggle even when the man dislocated his hip (Genesis 32:25), showing a determination that does not waver in the face of pain.
3. Figuratively, to struggle means to resist a superior force or an overwhelming reality, not to achieve definitive victory, but to hold firm and obtain a blessing.
H0079.origine: The Hebrew verb אָבַק (avaq) evokes the idea of dust (עָבָק, avaq as a noun): the close combat raises dust, hence the image of intense and dusty grappling. The etymology suggests a confused, swirling action, where two bodies confront each other in a cloud of dust. It is a rare verb, primarily attested to describe decisive wrestling matches.
H0079.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Bible, both in the account of Genesis 32:24-25, where Jacob struggles with a mysterious man at night, before receiving the name Israel. The context shows an unequal but fierce struggle: Jacob refuses to let go even after being injured. The word makes tangible the intensity of the fight, not a mere abstract spiritual trial, but a real physical confrontation that forever marks the one who endures it.
H0079.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that the encounter with God can involve intense struggle, not passive submission. Jacob does not yield even in the face of a superhuman force: he struggles, he resists, he asks for a blessing. This image shows that faith does not exclude effort, tenacity, or even inner combat before God. For the Christian, it speaks to the necessity of persevering in prayer and commitment, even when it costs.

sens: Fine particles of earth or matter lifted and floating in the air
Powdered material, reduced to fine powder
Image of lightness, fragility, and transience
Cloud, mist raised by the wind or a great multitude
H0080.detail: 1. Dust in its primary sense refers to the collection of fine particles of earth or matter that float in the air and settle everywhere, lifted by the wind or movement. In Exodus 9:9, during the sixth plague of Egypt, dust becomes a force of divine judgment, covering the entire land and causing sores on men and animals. 2. By extension, it also refers to fine powder in general, the residue reduced to tiny grains. When the Lord threatens Israel in Deuteronomy 28:24, He sends dust instead of rain, a symbol of sterility and curse. 3. Figuratively, dust represents fragility and insignificance: in Isaiah 5:24, the flower of the wicked "will dissipate like dust," meaning it will disappear without a trace, so light and fleeting it is. 4. Finally, a multitude that raises dust evokes the tumult, the confusion of a great army in motion: in Isaiah 29:5, the numerous enemies are described as "fine dust," or in Nahum 1:3, the clouds are "the dust of His feet," a poetic image of God's overwhelming power and presence.
H0080.origine: The Hebrew word אָבָק (avaq) primarily denotes the common natural phenomenon: the earth being lifted. Its etymology suggests the idea of agitation and dispersion. In biblical Hebrew, the word is infrequent but always carries a symbolic or dramatic weight, never neutral — it appears in contexts of divine judgment, destruction, or overwhelming power.
H0080.emploi: The word אָבָק appears six times in the Hebrew Bible and is found exclusively in solemn contexts. In Exodus 9:9, it is one of the plagues of Egypt. In Deuteronomy 28:24, it is part of the curses of Sinai. In the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Nahum), dust symbolizes either the destruction and dispersion of the wicked (Isaiah 5:24), the tumult of an invading army (Ezekiel 26:10, Isaiah 29:5), or the impressive manifestation of divine power (Nahum 1:3). The term thus oscillates between a physical reality and an image of judgment, finitude, or majesty.
H0080.portee: Meditating on the dust we are (according to Genesis 3:19) helps the Christian recognize their fragility and nothingness before God. This biblical image calls them to humility and trust in the One whose power crushes the forces that rise against them. It also reminds us that all human power, all pride, dissipates like dust in the wind.

sens: Powder or fragrant substance, generally derived from plants or resins, used in religious rituals, cosmetics, or trade
Collection of perfumes and incense burned or used to create a pleasant smell
H0081.detail:
1. The word refers to an aromatic powder, often extracted from exotic plants or precious resins. It is a valuable, costly substance that emits a pleasant odor. In Song of Solomon 3:6, the author describes a royal procession coming up from the desert "amid the vapors of myrrh and incense and all the aromatic substances of the merchants": these substances were imported by merchants and represented luxury and elegance.
2. By extension, the word can refer to the collection of perfumes burned or used during solemn ceremonies, creating a noble and pleasant atmosphere. The image evokes the fragrant smoke that rises during important rituals or festive moments.
H0081.origine: The Hebrew word אֲבָקָה comes from a root that evokes fine powder and the idea of breaking, reducing to powder. It is related to other Hebrew words denoting dust or fine particles. The word fits within the semantic field of precious substances in the Middle East: myrrh, incense, aloes, used both for worship and for the daily lives of high-ranking individuals.
H0081.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 3:6. The context clearly indicates that it refers to luxury substances imported by merchants, associated with wealth, beauty, and solemnity. Its unique use suggests that the author of the Song chose rare and exotic terms to evoke an atmosphere of royal splendor and sensual allure.
H0081.portee: This word reminds the reader that perfume and pleasant scents held an important place in the lives of high-ranking Israelites and in their relationships with God. Aromatic substances also evoke prayer, worship, and precious moments with the Lord, where all our senses participate in worship. It is an invitation not to reduce faith to a purely mental affair: it also encompasses beauty, sensitivity, and the joy of the senses.

sens: To move in the air by flapping wings
(figuratively) To soar quickly
H0082.detail:
1. The word describes the movement of a bird that propels itself into the air by spreading and flapping its wings. It is the characteristic action of birds in flight. In Job 39:29, it speaks of the majestic flight of the hawk that "spreads its wings toward the south," evoking its graceful and powerful ascent into the sky.
2. In a figurative sense, the word can evoke any quick and light action, like a movement that rises or escapes swiftly. The image of wings beating the air suggests dynamism and freedom of movement.
H0082.origine: The Hebrew word אָבַר (abar) belongs to the family of verbs that describe the movements of birds. The form used here is the Hiphil (a causative form), which intensifies the idea of active and energetic movement. The base image is that of wing beats: abar evokes the action of traversing the air in continuous motion, like birds piercing the space with the movement of their wings.
H0082.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 39:29, in the context of God's discourse to Job about wild creatures. There, it specifically describes the flight of the hawk, a bird of prey known for its majesty and power. God asks Job how man, with all his supposed intelligence, could understand or order the instinctive behavior of creatures? The flight of the hawk thus becomes an illustration of the divine wisdom inscribed in creation, beyond what human intelligence can master.
H0082.portee: This word reminds us that God has endowed creatures with instincts and abilities that we cannot create or truly understand. The majestic flight of the hawk speaks to us of God's creative power and our smallness in the face of the mysteries of creation. It is an invitation to humility and wonder before the work of God.

sens: A bird's wing, part of the body that allows it to fly
Movement, action of flying
Protection, refuge offered to one who takes shelter
H0083.detail:
1. The wing is primarily the natural organ of the bird: the dove has delicate wings, the eagle has powerful and majestic wings. This is what the psalmist evokes when he says, "if I had the wings of a dove, I would fly away" (Psalms 55:7) — he dreams of escaping his enemies with the lightness and speed of a bird.
2. The wing also refers to the act of flying itself, the manner in which one moves in flight: those who trust in the Lord "will soar on wings like eagles" (Isaiah 40:31), meaning they rise high, with strength and confidence, without exhaustion.
3. Figuratively, the wing evokes protection and refuge: it is the image of the Babylonian king in Ezekiel 17:3, whose outstretched wings cover and dominate. The Bible also uses this image for God Himself, who places His creatures "in the shadow of His wings" (biblical references of divine protection).
H0083.origine: The Hebrew word אֵבֶר comes from a root that means "to fly" or "to surpass." It is a concrete word that primarily describes the visible and functional appendage of the bird. The same word is used for the wing of the sky, meaning its expanse: the wing of the space that the bird traverses. The family of the word includes terms related to movement and deployment.
H0083.emploi: The word appears three times in the provided passages. In poetry (Psalms 55:7), the psalmist uses this natural image to express his desire to escape from distress. In Isaiah 40:31, the religious context transforms the wing into a symbol of renewed strength through trust in God: it is no longer just an anatomical organ, but a capacity to rise spiritually. In Ezekiel 17:3, the eagle with outstretched wings represents political power (the Babylonian king), showing how the natural image metaphorically becomes a sign of domination and power. Each time, the meaning remains anchored in the concrete observation of the bird but is enriched with a moral or spiritual significance.
H0083.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on trust in God. When Isaiah speaks of soaring like eagles, he reminds us that those who surrender to God find new strength to overcome exhaustion and fatigue: it is a promise of renewal. The image of God's protective wings also reveals His care for His children, offering comfort to those who feel threatened or fragile.

sens: Feather or wing of a bird
The entire plumage of a bird
Protection and refuge offered by God (image)
H0084.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the feather or wing of a bird — what covers the body of the animal and allows it to fly. In Deuteronomy 32:11, the eagle "spreads its wings, takes them, and carries them on its feathers": it is the feather understood as part of the wing that the bird uses to carry its young. 2. By extension, it refers to the entire visible plumage, the external appearance of the bird adorned with its feathers. Psalm 68:14 speaks of "the wing of the dove" whose "plumage is of golden yellow": here, the word evokes the colorful beauty of the whole bird. 3. The word is also used figuratively to express divine protection. In Psalm 91:4, God "will cover you with His feathers" and you will find "refuge under His wings": it is no longer the real bird, but the image of a mother bird who envelops and protects her chicks — an image of complete security in God.
H0084.origine: The Hebrew word אֶבְרָה (evrah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering or veil. It is related to other Hebrew words concerning wings and feathers. The image is very concrete: it comes from the observable spectacle of the bird hiding its young under its wings, a gesture of natural protection that the Scriptures apply to God to express His maternal love for His people.
H0084.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in poetic contexts. In Deuteronomy 32:11, it describes the action of the eagle carrying its young on its feathers — a concrete example of the bird's maternal behavior. In Job 39:16 and Psalms 68:14, it refers to the visible and splendid plumage of different birds (ostrich, stork, dove). In Psalms 91:4, the meaning becomes entirely figurative: the feathers become the symbol of absolute divine protection. The word always remains connected to the vivid image of the bird, never abstract.
H0084.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on God's protection. The image of the hen who envelops her chicks under her wings, which Jesus Himself will later refer to (Matthew 23:37), conveys that God desires to cover us completely, to keep us safe from danger. It is a word of consolation and trust: whoever seeks refuge in God will find complete and tender security.

sens: The patriarch founder of the people of Israel
The man who received God's covenant and the promise of an innumerable descendants
The one in whom the transformation of his name is fulfilled (from Abram to Abraham)
The exemplary figure of faith and obedience to God
H0085.detail:
1. Abraham is the patriarch — the founding father — of the people of Israel and of biblical faith. His story occupies a central place in Genesis (chapters 11 to 25), as he is the father of Isaac, from whom the Hebrew people descend. He represents the beginning of the chosen nation.

2. God establishes an eternal covenant with Abraham and promises him descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky or the grains of sand: "for I have made you a father of many nations" (Genesis 17:5). This promise remains at the heart of the faith of Israel and the Christian Church throughout Scripture.

3. His name itself changes: from Abram ("exalted father") to Abraham ("father of a multitude"), a sign that God transforms the one He calls and fulfills His word (Genesis 17:5).

4. Abraham becomes the living example of faith: he leaves his land in obedience to God's call, and later he even accepts to sacrifice his son Isaac, believing that God will keep His promises. This act of trust, described in Genesis 22, establishes him as a model of one who fully believes in God.
H0085.origine: The name Abraham literally means "father of a multitude" or "father of nations." The Bible itself explains this meaning at the moment when God changes Abram's name to Abraham (Genesis 17:5). This name change marks a turning point in the history of salvation: it symbolizes that God transforms the person He calls and fulfills His promise Himself. Before this change, he was called Abram (הברא in Hebrew), whose meaning is less clearly universal.
H0085.emploi: Abraham appears 173 times in the Bible, almost entirely in Genesis (chapters 11 to 25). His story begins in Genesis 11:26, where he is introduced as the son of Terah and the brother of Nahor and Haran. God calls him to leave Ur of the Chaldeans, and Abraham obeys. The Bible recounts his journeys in Canaan, his marriage to Sarah, the miraculous birth of Isaac despite his wife's advanced age, and the sacrifice of Isaac commanded and then stopped by God (Genesis 22). Abraham dies at 175 years old and is buried in Hebron. His name also appears in Deuteronomy and in the Psalms, where Moses and the psalmist call upon God, remembering the covenant made with Abraham (Deuteronomy 9:27). In the New Testament, Jesus Himself invokes Abraham as the father of believers, and the apostle Paul makes him the living proof that salvation comes by faith, not by works of the Law.
H0085.portee: Abraham teaches the believer that faith is not primarily an intellectual belief, but a concrete obedience: he leaves his country not knowing where he is going, believing God's word. His story also shows that God fulfills His promises even when everything seems impossible: Sarah gives birth at 90 years old. Finally, Abraham becomes for every Christian a model of radical trust in God, particularly through his acceptance of the sacrifice of Isaac, where he renounces his greatest earthly good to remain faithful to God.

sens: Order to bow before someone
Gesture of homage or submission
H0086.detail:
1. The word refers to the act of bending the knees, a gesture of respect or reverence towards a person of high rank. It is a cry announced to proclaim the solemn arrival of Joseph in Egypt: "Kneel!" means that the crowd must prostrate themselves before him (Genesis 41:43).
2. Figuratively, it is the physical expression of submission and homage. Bending the knees before someone acknowledges their authority and greatness — in this case, the new authority that Pharaoh entrusts to Joseph over all the land.
H0086.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that originally means "to bend" or "to bow." The related Aramaic (אַרְכֻבָּה) directly refers to the knee, the joint of the body. This same root is found in other words of the family that express the inclination or bending of the body. The gesture of the knee was in the ancient Near East a universal language of respect towards royal or divine power.
H0086.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the account of Joseph's exaltation. Pharaoh, after recognizing Joseph as a man filled with the Spirit of God, appoints him as the vice-regent of Egypt. The cry "Kneel!" (or "Knee!") is shouted before his chariot so that all the people pay homage to this new authority. It is a decisive moment where Joseph, once a slave, receives honor and power.
H0086.portee: This passage shows that honor and respect come from God alone. Joseph did not ask for anything: it is God who elevated him, and the honors that Joseph receives reveal that God can elevate a righteous person even in the heart of a foreign land. For the believer, it is an image of divine promotion — one who forgets themselves and serves faithfully can be elevated, not by their own strength, but by the hand of God.

sens: Hebrew patriarch of the second millennium before Christ
Founding father of the people of Israel and believers in God
Man of unwavering faith despite repeated trials
H0087.detail:
1. Abram is a historical figure in the Bible, living in the time of the patriarchs, born in Ur before settling in Canaan. He first appears in Genesis 11:26 as the son of Terach, brother of Nahor and Haran, and husband of Sarai (Gen 11:29).
2. He becomes the founding patriarch of the Hebrew people: God promises him a numerous descendants and the land of Canaan, although he is childless (Gen 15:2-3). Abram receives this promise "by believing in the Lord" (Gen 15:6), which establishes the biblical faith.
3. His name, Abram, means "exalted father" in Hebrew. In Genesis 17:5, God changes his name to Abraham, "father of a multitude of nations," marking the fulfillment of the promise and his universal role in salvation.
H0087.origine: The name Abram comes from the Hebrew אַבְרָם, composed of the root אַב ("father") and the word רַם ("exalted, elevated"). It expresses the idea of eminent fatherhood. This name is changed to Abraham (אַבְרָהָם) in Genesis 17:5, meaning "father of a multitude," which becomes the patriarch's definitive name throughout the Bible.
H0087.emploi: Abram appears as the personal name of the patriarch in chapters 11 to 17 of Genesis, and then in genealogical references (1 Chronicles 1:27, Nehemiah 9:7). It is the name he bears before his covenant with God in Genesis 17. The narratives show him accumulating wealth (Gen 13:2), building altars to worship the Lord (Gen 12:7), rescuing his nephew Lot (Gen 14:14), and waiting for years for the promised child (Gen 15:2-3). After Genesis 17:5, the text normally uses the name Abraham, marking the transformation of the character by divine grace.
H0087.portee: Abram embodies the power of faith in God even before possessing what is promised to him. His story teaches the believer that trust in God is the foundation of the relationship with Him, not works or circumstances. This is why the apostle Paul cites him as an example of justification by faith (Romans 4). His call to leave his land for a distant promise remains a model of radical commitment to God.

sens: Stage in the desert where the Israelites camped during their exodus
Location situated east of Moab, near the border
H0088.detail: 1. Oboth is a place mentioned four times in the Bible, always in relation to the journey of the Israelites in the desert after their departure from Egypt. It is a stop on their long journey to the Promised Land, where they camped (Numbers 21:10-11). 2. The site was located east of Moab, marking an important point as they approached the Moabite border (Numbers 33:44). Its exact location remains uncertain, but it represented a significant geographical landmark on the desert route.
H0088.origine: The name Oboth literally means "water skins" or "water reservoirs" in Hebrew, likely evoking a vital source or well of water in this arid desert territory. This designation suggests that the place was known for its access to water, a precious and crucial resource for desert travelers.
H0088.emploi: Oboth is mentioned only in the accounts of the desert journey of the children of Israel. It appears in two parallel passages: the narrative account in Numbers 21:10-11, where the Israelites depart from Oboth to head towards Ijjé-Abarim (on the eastern side of Moab), and the list of stages in the itinerary in Numbers 33:43-44, which enumerates all the desert camps. The site marks a stop located after Punon and just before the Moabite border.

sens: Father of the warrior Shammah, one of David's mighty men
H0089.detail: Agué is a man from the time of the united monarchy in Israel, known only for being the father of Shammah. Shammah is mentioned among the "mighty men" or heroes of David (2 Samuel 23:11), these elite warriors who served the king with distinction. The text designates him as "Shammah, son of Agué, from Harar," which also indicates that Agué or his family came from the region of Harar.
H0089.origine: The name Agué means "I will multiply" or "I will increase," expressing the idea of increase and growth. It is a typical theophoric name in biblical Hebrew, likely constructed on the root meaning "great" or "to grow."
H0089.emploi: Agué appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 23:11, in the list of renowned warriors serving King David. He is presented solely as the father of Shammah, who distinguished himself during a battle against the Philistines at Lehi, where he valiantly defended a field of lentils.

sens: King of Amalek during the time of Saul
H0090G.detail: Agag is the king of the Amalekite people mentioned in the prophecy of Balaam (Numbers 24:7). His name literally means "I will dominate" or "I will surpass," evoking pride and domination. In this prophetic verse, Balaam contemplates the future power of the people of Israel and says: "His king rises above Agag, and his kingdom becomes powerful" — meaning that Israel will surpass even the formidable king Agag and dominate over him.
H0090G.origine: The name Agag means "the one who dominates" or "I will dominate" in Hebrew, reflecting the pride and power of the king of Amalek. This name seems to have been used as a royal title among Amalekite kings, somewhat like "Pharaoh" in Egypt. It is a name that inspires fear and symbolizes the pride of an enemy nation of Israel.
H0090G.emploi: Agag appears only once in the received biblical usages, in Numbers 24:7, in the prophecy of Balaam. This non-Israelite prophet paradoxically blesses Israel despite Balak's efforts to have him curse it. Balaam announces that Israel will be greater and more powerful than King Agag, the feared ruler of the Amalekites. Although this entry is limited to this unique usage, the name of this king reappears elsewhere in the history of Israel, particularly during the confrontation between Saul and Samuel.
H0090G.portee: This prophecy reminds us that the enemies of Israel — even powerful ones like Agag and the Amalekites — cannot surpass the divine blessing on God's people. It shows that true greatness comes from God, not from human pride or military strength. It is an encouragement for the believer: their security rests not on their own domination, but on faithfulness to God.

sens: King of Amalek during the time of the united monarchy in Israel
Symbol of pride and disobedience to God
H0090H.detail:
1. Agag is a king of Amalek who lived during the time of King Saul of Israel. When Saul fights the Amalekites at God's command, he captures Agag alive instead of killing him as commanded (1 Samuel 15:8-9). Agag then approaches the prophet Samuel "cheerfully," unaware that he is about to die (1 Samuel 15:32).

2. The name Agag embodies human pride that refuses to fully obey God. Saul spares the enemy king and the best of the spoils against the explicit command of the Lord, which leads to his condemnation as king (1 Samuel 15:20-23). Samuel then executes Agag "before the Lord" while declaring a prophetic sentence (1 Samuel 15:33).
H0090H.origine: The name means "I will surpass" or "I will dominate" in Hebrew, expressing the characteristic arrogance of this king. The Amalekites are an ancient people, historical enemies of Israel, hence the name "Agagite" (אֲגָגִי) applied to Esther's enemy, Haman, who presents himself as a descendant of this lineage. The word reflects the pride of the warrior that only divine will can bring down.
H0090H.emploi: Agag appears five times in the account of 1 Samuel 15, concentrated in a few verses. He is a historical figure from the time of Saul, the king of Amalek captured alive in battle (1 Samuel 15:8). The account emphasizes that Saul spares him despite the divine order (1 Samuel 15:9, 15:20), and Samuel puts him to death as judgment for this disobedience (1 Samuel 15:33). Agag also appears indirectly through the term "Agagite" applied to Haman, the persecutor of the Jews under King Ahasuerus, marking the continuity of the conflict between the descendants of Amalek and Israel.
H0090H.portee: The story of Agag teaches that obedience to God must be complete and uncompromising, even towards a captive enemy. Saul's sparing of Agag despite the divine order, for the sake of military glory or spoils, leads to Saul's rejection as king. This story highlights that God's will is non-negotiable, and that Christians must examine the areas where they yield to the temptation to "keep" what God asks them to abandon.

sens: Descendant of Agag, king mentioned during the time of the united monarchy in Israel
H0091.detail: The Agagite is someone who descends from Agag, an important figure during the time of King Saul. The term specifically refers to Haman, minister of King Ahasuerus (Persia), whom the text repeatedly qualifies as an "Agagite" (Esther 3:1 and 3:10). This genealogy connects him to the ancient royalty of Amalek, a historical enemy of Israel.
H0091.origine: The word comes directly from the proper name Agag (אֲגָג), a king of Amalek captured by King Saul during a battle against this people (1 Samuel 15:8). The Hebrew suffix adds the idea of belonging or descent. The name Agag itself means "I will surpass" or "I will be exalted," expressing pride and ambition.
H0091.emploi: The term "Agagite" appears only five times in the Bible, exclusively in the book of Esther, and always refers to Haman. The repetition of this qualifier (Esther 3:1, 3:10, 8:3, 8:5, 9:24) emphasizes his identity and hostility towards the Jews. By calling him "Agagite," the biblical text establishes a link between Haman and the ancient enemy of Israel, Agag: it shows that the hatred of the Jews did not originate with Haman, but is part of a long chain of hostility between Amalek (the people of Agag) and Israel.

sens: Cord or knotted object used for tying
Group of people united or forming a group
Chain of servitude or oppression
Vault or celestial structure that supports the world
H0092.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a physical link, a rope or cord: in Exodus 12:22, a "bunch" of hyssop (branches tied together) is dipped in blood to mark the doors. It is the image of things attached or knotted together.
2. It applies to a group of people united or organized: in 2 Samuel 2:25, the sons of Benjamin "formed a body," meaning they gathered into a coherent, tight troop like a bundle.
3. It evokes the idea of binding links: in Isaiah 58:6, the prophet speaks of "undoing the bonds of servitude," an image of the moral and social chains that oppress. It is the same word, but used in the figurative sense of what enslaves.
4. In Amos 9:6, it describes the "vault" of the heavens—the structure that "binds" heaven to earth, which supports and maintains the universe in place. It is the cosmic link that organizes creation.
H0092.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to bind" or "to tighten." It denotes everything that binds, ties, or assembles: ropes, bands, and by extension, anything that forms a compact whole. The basic image is that of a knot or bundle. The word can express both a material physical link and a social (a troop) or cosmic (a structure that supports) link, but always with the idea of assembly and cohesion.
H0092.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. Its usage varies according to context: in Exodus 12:22, it is a concrete object (a tied bunch); in 2 Samuel 2:25, it is a group of soldiers; in Isaiah 58:6, it is an image of oppression and spiritual or social bondage; in Amos 9:6, it is a description of cosmic order. The word thus oscillates between literal and figurative meaning, but always retains the underlying idea of assembly, binding, or structure that holds things together.
H0092.portee: This word invites the reader to perceive how God creates and maintains the order of the world—whether physical, social, or spiritual—through "links" that bind together. It can also evoke the bondage of sin as a set of chains to be broken (Isaiah), reminding us that true liberation consists of untying those bonds that enslave. The notion of "link" remains central to biblical theology: links of creation, links of community, links of oppression from which only the Lord can free us.

sens: the tree that produces nuts
the wood of this tree, often used in carpentry
figuratively, a garden or orchard
H0093.detail: 1. The walnut tree is the tree that bears nuts, a prized fruit for its nutritious kernel. It is a sturdy tree with beautiful foliage, often planted in the orchards of the ancient Near East. In the Song of Solomon, the beloved descends into a "garden of walnuts" to admire the greenery of the valley and see if the vine and pomegranates are in bloom (Song of Solomon 6:11)—it is a place of delight, strolling, and observing the fruitful nature. 2. Walnut wood, hard and beautiful, was also valued in antiquity for making furniture and precious objects. 3. In this passage from the Song, the walnut orchard represents a space of natural beauty and joy, where one contemplates the fruits and growth of plants.
H0093.origine: The Hebrew word אֱגוֹז (egoz) simply refers to the walnut tree and its fruit. It is borrowed from an ancient Semitic root. This word appears infrequently in the Bible, as walnuts are not as abundant in Israel as in colder regions, but it evokes a tree known and appreciated for the quality of its fruit and wood.
H0093.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Solomon 6:11. It is used in the plural to refer to a grove or thicket of walnuts—not merely as a fruit tree, but as a bucolic setting where the beauty of creation is manifested and where the beloved enjoys strolling. It is a vocabulary of luxury and delight, emphasizing the abundance and joy of nature.
H0093.portee: The walnut tree, in this context of the Song of Solomon, invites the reader to savor the simple beauty of creation—the trees, fruits, flowers—as an expression of love and joy. It is a call to contemplate what God has made for our pleasure and nourishment.

sens: Wise author of maxims mentioned only once in the Bible
H0094.detail: Agur is a wise man who lived during the time of the united Israelite monarchy. He is known only from Proverbs 30:1, where he presents himself as the author or compiler of a series of sayings and maxims. His name means "one who has gathered," which fits well with his role as a collector of wise words intended to instruct Ithiel and those who listen to him.
H0094.origine: The name Agur derives from a Hebrew root meaning "to gather" or "to assemble." This reflects his function: he gathered and organized words of wisdom. His father Jake is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible. The name "Agur" thus suggests a man who has collected and transmitted the teachings of the wise.
H0094.emploi: Agur is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 30:1. Little is known about his life, except that he is the son of Jake and that he spoke a series of sayings and maxims addressed to Ithiel. These words, which occupy chapter 30 of Proverbs, form a varied collection of advice and observations on life, nature, and human conduct. Although little known, Agur contributed to the treasure of biblical wisdom.

sens: A small coin, a piece of silver
A small wage or gain, a modest remuneration
H0095.detail:
1. A coin of low value, a small metal coin — in this case, a piece of silver. It is a concrete monetary unit that can be held in hand and given or received. In 1 Samuel 2:36, the fallen members of Eli's family came begging for a piece of silver, showing how precious this currency was for the poor.
2. By extension, the wage or gain derived from work, especially a modest or humiliating gain. In the same verse, receiving a piece of silver meant accepting a small remuneration in exchange for a priestly charge, marking the fall of Eli's house: great priests reduced to begging for bread and small coins.
H0095.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root that designates the action of monetizing or dividing into parts. It refers to a struck or cast coin of small value, common enough to be given as payment or alms. This word reflects the simple monetary exchanges of the ancient Near East, where the coin was one of the most common forms of payment.
H0095.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Samuel 2:36. It designates a currency of little value that the impoverished members of the high priest Eli's family were reduced to begging for. The context emphasizes the downfall: once privileged in worship, they came to beg for a simple piece of silver and a piece of bread. This passage illustrates how divine curse on Eli's house manifested through the loss of its wealth and prestige.
H0095.portee: This account reminds us that wealth and position, even those acquired through sacred service, are not assured if one turns away from God. The fall of Eli's house from prosperity to begging for a simple coin shows the gravity of divine judgment on unfaithfulness and contempt for His word. For the reader, it is an invitation to fear God and to faithfulness, knowing that God exercises His judgment even on those who hold the highest religious offices.

sens: Fine particle of liquid that falls
H0096.detail: 1. A small quantity of liquid that forms and falls, like a drop of water or dew — the image of a tiny particle detached from the whole. In Job 38:28, God poses the rhetorical question: "Does rain have a father? Who gives birth to the drops of dew?" — it is the drop of dew that covers the grass in the morning, the smallest visible unit of water from the heavens.
H0096.origine: The Hebrew word אֵגֶל (egel) primarily designates a small drop, presumably formed from a root expressing the idea of "to detach" or "to fall." It is a concrete and simple term, without complex etymology, referring to the common observation of nature: this droplet that detaches and falls.
H0096.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Job 38:28. It is found in this sublime passage where God questions Job about the mysteries of creation: the cycle of rain, the birth of dew, who is responsible? It is in this context of divine majesty that the drop becomes the image of the infinitely small, of what only God can generate and control.
H0096.portee: This small drop reminds us that God reigns over the most humble and ordinary realities — not only over the great elements of the cosmos but also over every drop of dew that sparkles in the morning. It is an invitation to recognize divine providence even in the imperceptible details of nature.

sens: City of Moab
H0097.detail: Églaïm is a city located in the territory of Moab, beyond the Jordan. Its name literally means "double reservoir," likely evoking the presence of significant wells or cisterns in this region.
H0097.origine: The name Églaïm comes from Hebrew and means "double reservoir": it combines a word designating a reservoir or cistern with an indication of duality (the double). This type of geographical name often reflects a notable characteristic of the place — here, likely the existence of essential water reservoirs in this region of the Moab plateau.
H0097.emploi: Églaïm appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 15:8, in a passage where the prophet depicts divine judgment on Moab. The mention of this city is part of a list of Moabite localities that will be struck, highlighting the extent of the catastrophe that will affect the entire region.

sens: Stagnant body of water, natural or formed by the accumulation of water
Troubled, muddy, or marshy water
Marsh, wetland covered with reeds and bulrushes
Place transformed by divine power, symbol of fertility in the desert
H0098.detail:
1. A pond is a stagnant body of water — smaller than a lake, often shallow — where water accumulates naturally or through dams. In Egypt, during the plagues, the ponds of the Nile were turned into blood (Exodus 7:19).
2. The word also designates troubled, muddy, or gloomy water, particularly marshes where water stagnates and darkens. The Lord commanded Aaron to bring up the frogs from the Egyptian ponds (Exodus 8:1).
3. A pond is often covered with reeds and bulrushes — these plants that grow at the edge of the water and moist soil. Isaiah 35:7 announces that in the dry desert, reeds and bulrushes will grow, transforming the parched land.
4. In biblical theology, the pond symbolizes divine transformation: Psalm 107:35 celebrates how God "turns the desert into a pond," and Psalm 114:8 how He turns "the rock into a pond" — an image of His creative power that brings forth life where dryness reigns.
H0098.origine: The Hebrew word agam comes from a root expressing the idea of gathering or stagnation. The word generally translates what accumulates or stops, like water that does not flow. In the Bible, this word appears mostly in the poetic and prophetic passages of the Old Testament, where it describes both natural waters and the miraculous transformations performed by God.
H0098.emploi: The word agam appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 7:19 and 8:1) where the ponds become the setting for God's miracles. It also appears widely in the prophets — Isaiah (14:23, 35:7, 41:18, 42:15) and Jeremiah (51:32) — where it evokes either the drying up of judgment or the creation of new life in the desert. The meaning varies: sometimes an ordinary pond, sometimes an unpleasant marsh, sometimes a sign of divine fertility.
H0098.portee: For the believer, the pond reminds us that God controls all things, even waters that seem stagnant or useless — He makes them instruments of judgment or grace. This image invites the reader to see in the most improbable transformations the hand of the Lord creating new life in the very heart of the arid desert of existence.

sens: Affected by sadness or grief
Downcast, discouraged in feelings
Oppressed by inner affliction
H0099.detail:
1. The word expresses a state of deep affliction, like the soul that is saddened by misfortune or loss. In Isaiah 19:10, the Egyptian mercenaries are "saddened" upon seeing the economic collapse of the country during the plagues: they lose their livelihood and their hope.
2. More broadly, it denotes a heart that is oppressed, weighed down by the burden of circumstances. It is less a fleeting sadness than a lasting dejection, which affects the entire soul and paralyzes one's strength.
3. The word also evokes the idea of being broken internally, emptied of all comfort — a state where grief has removed all desire to act or hope.
H0099.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the image of a pond or stagnant water: something that no longer flows, that festers. By extension, it applies to the soul or feelings that "stagnate" in dejection, frozen in grief and unable to rise again. It is a very concrete image: like dead water, the saddened soul no longer circulates, no longer truly lives.
H0099.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 19:10, in the context of the plagues of Egypt. It depicts the humiliation of the workers and Egyptian mercenaries who, after the destruction of the crops (flax, barley), find themselves without work and resources. The sadness does not come from an internal cause, but from external ruin: it is the helplessness in the face of calamities that weighs down the soul.
H0099.portee: This word reminds us that grief and dejection can paralyze our strength — but also that God uses these moments of distress to show His power and call men to recognize Him. The Egyptian mercenaries, in their affliction, should have seen the hand of the God of Israel. For the believer, sadness is never the final word: it is an opportunity to turn to God.
